articles.title: The Persistence of US Trade Remedies Against China
articles.full_text:
Leader-level diplomacy gives the impression that the U.S. “trade war” has ended. That’s far from the truth.
Recent China-U.S. trade negotiations raised hopes that economic ties may be stabilizing after years of escalating tensions. A key milestone was U.S. President Donald Trump’s state visit to China in mid-May 2026, during which he and President Xi Jinping explicitly agreed to build a “constructive relationship of strategic stability” based on “fairness and reciprocity.” 
Yet the ongoing negotiations have done little to alter the institutional machinery of U.S. trade policy toward China. Behind the headlines, anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations, together with recurring “sunset reviews,” continue to advance under established statutory procedures.
During Trump’s visit to China, Beijing and Washington reached preliminary agreements on tariffs, market access, investment, and critical mineral supply chains, raising hopes of stabilizing bilateral economic relations. Yet the negotiations left the U.S. trade remedy regime untouched.
The U.S. Department of Commerce and U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) have continued anti-dumping, countervailing duty, and five-year sunset review proceedings against Chinese goods pursuant to established statutory procedures. Most trade remedy measures remain in place despite the recent easing of tensions. As Chad Bown observed, their continued operation reflects how deeply these measures are embedded in U.S. legal and political institutions, making meaningful reform difficult. 
In short, recent negotiations have eased short-term trade tensions without changing the institutional foundations of U.S. trade policy toward China. These trade remedy mechanisms generate far longer-lasting bilateral economic friction than tariffs subject to diplomatic bargaining. That much is clear from recent USITC data.
These data suggest that the U.S. trade remedies have become increasingly institutionalized, with China as the central focus of the system. Between January and June 2026, the USITC initiated 183 trade remedy investigations, 72 of which involved products from mainland China or Hong Kong, accounting for nearly 40 percent of all cases. The breadth of these investigations is equally striking. They included 37 anti-dumping cases, 27 countervailing duty cases, 14 Section 337 investigations, and 21 five-year sunset reviews, illustrating that China is subject to virtually every major U.S. trade remedy instrument. 
Among completed cases, 57 resulted in affirmative determinations, while only two produced negative findings, highlighting the durability rather than temporary nature of existing trade restrictions. These figures indicate that trade restrictions have evolved beyond case-by-case enforcement into a stable, institutionalized system governing U.S. trade policy toward China.
Among U.S. trade remedy instruments, five-year sunset reviews most clearly illustrate the path dependence of U.S. trade policy towards China. These reviews were originally designed to determine whether existing anti-dumping and countervailing duty measures should expire (“sunset”) after five years. Yet in practice, the review process has functioned as a mechanism for maintaining existing restrictions rather than terminating them. Once trade remedy orders are incorporated into domestic legal procedures, their continuation becomes easier than their removal.
According to the USITC database, 21 China-related cases have entered the sunset review process, with many proceeding to second or even third rounds of review. Some products, including preserved mushrooms, non-oriented electrical steel, and citric acid and “certain citrate salts,” have remained subject to U.S. trade remedy measures for more than two decades. In practice, sunset reviews have evolved from an exit mechanism into a mechanism for policy continuity, reinforcing the durability of U.S. trade restrictions against China. 
The industrial distribution of recent investigations also reflects changing U.S. policy priorities. Whereas trade remedies historically focused on traditional manufacturing sectors such as steel and aluminum, recent investigations increasingly target higher-value and strategically important industries, such as pharmaceuticals, chemicals, automotive manufacturing, semiconductors, electronic components, and advanced machinery. Chemicals and pharmaceuticals alone account for approximately 20 investigations – nearly one-third of all China-related cases.
This shift mirrors broader U.S. industrial policies, including the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act. It suggests that trade remedies have become steadily aligned with broader industrial and technological competition rather than serving solely as tools to addressing individual trade disputes.
Another notable trend is the growing interaction among different trade policy instruments. Anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations remain the principal mechanisms for restricting Chinese imports. Although Section 337 investigations (dealing with “claims regarding intellectual property rights, including allegations of patent infringement and trademark infringement by imported goods”) accounted for only 14 cases, they were concentrated in technology-intensive products, including semiconductors, smart devices, and photovoltaic components. 
Recent USITC investigations involving semiconductor devices, TOPCon solar cells, and smart televisions illustrate how intellectual property enforcement has become closely intertwined with broader trade policy objectives. As Jennifer Hillman has argued, trade remedies are no longer simply instruments for correcting unfair trade practices; they increasingly serve broader industrial and strategic objectives.
Taken together, these developments suggest that U.S. trade remedies have evolved beyond temporary policy tools into an institutionalized framework for entrenched strategic competition with China.
The Impact of Persistent U.S. Trade Remedies on Chinese Firms
The most immediate consequence of persistent U.S. trade remedies has been a substantial increase in compliance costs for Chinese exporters. Once an anti-dumping or countervailing duty order is issued, it becomes subject to statutory review procedures rather than discretionary political adjustment. 
According to the Department of Commerce, companies participating in anti-dumping/countervailing duty proceedings are required to submit extensive documentation through its ACCESS system and remain subject to repeated administrative reviews that may establish new cash-deposit rates for future imports. The Department currently administers more than 700 anti-dumping/countervailing duty orders covering products from over 60 countries, underscoring the long-term and resource-intensive compliance burden facing firms involved in trade remedy proceedings. The burden falls disproportionately on small and medium-sized enterprises.
As a result, some Chinese exporters have scaled back or completely exited the U.S. market. What began as temporary remedies have thus become structural, long-term compliance burdens.
Beyond raising costs, persistent trade remedies have significantly increased uncertainty for Chinese exporters. Because anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations can remain in force for many years, firms face prolonged uncertainty over future duty rates, pricing strategies, and market access. The possibility of additional duty liabilities also affects importers’ behavior, with many reducing orders, delaying procurement, or seeking alternative suppliers once investigations initiated.
Chinese manufacturers such as LONGi, JinkoSolar, and Trina Solar have faced repeated U.S. anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations over a decade. Despite remaining globally competitive, recurring trade remedy proceedings have increased compliance burdens and accelerated adjustments to their global production networks. As a result, trade remedy risks have become an integral factor in corporate decision-making. For many exporters, uncertainty surrounding future investigations now carries consequences comparable to tariff increases themselves.
Rather than fundamentally constraining Chinese firms, persistent U.S. trade remedies have accelerated their strategic adjustment in global markets. Chinese firms have responded through market diversification, production network restructuring, and technological upgrading. As Rhodium Group observed, Chinese firms are progressively diversifying production across Asia without relocating their core industrial capabilities abroad. ASEAN remained China’s largest trading partner in 2025, with bilateral trade growing by 9.6 percent, while Belt and Road Initiative partner countries accounted for 51.8 percent of China’s foreign trade.
Many firms have also reconfigured their global production networks. Manufacturers in sectors such as electronics, photovoltaic products, and machinery have expanded production capacity in Southeast Asia, Mexico, and Central and Eastern Europe while retaining research and development, core technologies, and supply chain management in China. Chinese companies have announced nearly $400 billion in overseas clean-tech investment projects since 2014 across the EV, solar PV, and wind sectors. This approach reduces direct exposure to U.S. trade remedies while preserving China’s role in research, engineering, advanced manufacturing, and supply chain coordination.
At the same time, increasingly complex trade investigations have encouraged firms to strengthen their compliance capabilities and technological competitiveness. According to China’s General Administration of Customs, exports of mechanical and electrical products reached 7.8 trillion yuan in the first half of 2025, accounting for approximately 60 percent of China’s total exports. During the same period, exports of the country’s “new three” industries – new energy vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, and photovoltaic products – increased by 12.7 percent. Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency estimates that China accounts for more than 80 percent of global manufacturing capacity for photovoltaic modules, solar cells, and silicon wafers. Chinese firms are increasingly adjusting to a long-term institutionalized rather than temporary trade environment.
Recent negotiations have eased bilateral tensions, but they have not altered the underlying logic of U.S. trade remedy policy. While executive measures such as tariffs and export controls can be modified through political bargaining, anti-dumping and countervailing duty measures remain embedded in statutory procedures that are relatively insulated from diplomatic engagement. These measures have imposed significant costs on Chinese firms and reshaped their global strategies, yet they have not fundamentally undermined China’s broader industrial competitiveness. 
As Ryan Hass recently argued, the objective of contemporary China-U.S. engagement is less to eliminate competition than to manage it within acceptable boundaries. Looking ahead, China-U.S. economic relations are likely to continue along a dual-track dynamic: political dialogue may ease short-term tensions, while entrenched trade remedies remain a persistent source of bilateral economic friction. For now, the “sunset” remains largely procedural rather than substantive.
Recent China-U.S. trade negotiations raised hopes that economic ties may be stabilizing after years of escalating tensions. A key milestone was U.S. President Donald Trump’s state visit to China in mid-May 2026, during which he and President Xi Jinping explicitly agreed to build a “constructive relationship of strategic stability” based on “fairness and reciprocity.” 
Yet the ongoing negotiations have done little to alter the institutional machinery of U.S. trade policy toward China. Behind the headlines, anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations, together with recurring “sunset reviews,” continue to advance under established statutory procedures.
During Trump’s visit to China, Beijing and Washington reached preliminary agreements on tariffs, market access, investment, and critical mineral supply chains, raising hopes of stabilizing bilateral economic relations. Yet the negotiations left the U.S. trade remedy regime untouched.
The U.S. Department of Commerce and U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) have continued anti-dumping, countervailing duty, and five-year sunset review proceedings against Chinese goods pursuant to established statutory procedures. Most trade remedy measures remain in place despite the recent easing of tensions. As Chad Bown observed, their continued operation reflects how deeply these measures are embedded in U.S. legal and political institutions, making meaningful reform difficult.
articles.summary: Leader-level diplomacy gives the impression that the U.S. “trade war” has ended. That’s far from the truth.

articles.title: What a Stray Dog’s Murder Tells us About Chinese Civil Society
articles.full_text:
Wang Wang has appeared on billboards around the world – visible proof that China’s censorship does have limits.
A Wang Wang electronic billboard in Times Square, New York City.
In New York’s Times Square, a giant electronic billboard recently carried five words: “Never forget. Never give up.” Similar displays appeared near the Duomo in Milan, by the Leaning Tower of Pisa, and around Taipei 101, in a wave of memorials that hit more than 200 screens worldwide.
Ordinary Chinese people paid for these displays, one small donation at a time – all to mourn a stray dog.
On June 28, in a village in Jieyang, Guangdong, five boys — all under 14 years old — tortured and killed a stray mother dog, nicknamed Wang Wang by the villagers who knew her well, and her three puppies. They dragged her by a wire around her neck, beat her with sticks, doused her in fuel and set her alight. The boys laughed while they filmed it, then uploaded the footage to social media.
Because all four were below China’s age of criminal responsibility, the official response was to send them to a “specialized school” for corrective education. There were no formal charges – and not only because of their age. China still has no national statute against animal cruelty, so there was nothing to charge the boys with.
Nearly a month later, the case is still generating thousands of comments a day across Chinese social media. The shock, anger, and grief has coalesced into a concrete demand: pass an animal cruelty law.
Internet users carried that demand offline. They crowdfunded memorial displays on commercial LED screens in shopping districts across China. A domestic cosmetics brand even ran mall ads in Shenzhen: “Resist animal cruelty; insist there be a law to rely on.”
But China’s party-state is inordinately sensitive to popular movements that call for political change, even demand seemingly as innocuous as outlawing cruelty to animals. It didn’t take long for the censorship apparatus to kick in.
In Guangzhou, screens along Beijing Road pedestrian street that had carried Wang Wang displays went dark. Staff confirmed that they had been ordered to take the memorials down. Sympathy posts were quickly deleted from Weibo. In Chengdu, a street mural painted in Wang Wang’s memory was covered over. A leaked internal notice from a district internet affairs office in Shenyang reportedly classified the campaign demanding justice for Wang Wang as a “political risk” susceptible to “malicious hype by foreign forces,” and instructed officials to inspect commercial LED screens. 
The repression reach to Hong Kong, another symptom of the increasing restriction of free speech in the city. Internet users had crowdfunded a screen to display a Wang Wang memorial at the junction of Argyle and Shanghai Streets in Mong Kok. Handwritten placards appeared in Causeway Bay. Each display was shut down.

By that afternoon, the building’s management was demanding the banner come down, citing the lease. Leung complied. Then he cut the banner apart and rehung the fragments he could – the dogs’ portrait among them – inside his own window facing the street.
Days earlier, the adoption platform Suppaw had crowdfunded HK$95,000 (roughly US$12,000) in about two hours to place Wang Wang’s image on a Hong Kong tram. They were told that while the wording passed review, the images of the dogs did not — out of concern, the tram company said, that they might “affect public sentiment.”
With Wang Wang memorials tightly policed on the mainland and in Hong Kong, overseas billboards have become the only outlet left for public anger and grief.
Hong Kongers will recognize this playbook. In 2019, they crowdfunded newspaper ads in dozens of major dailies ahead of the G20 summit, asking the international community to stand with the movement against the extradition bill.
What is remarkable about the Wang Wang campaign is that this same model — horizontal, leaderless, funded in micro-donations, executed across jurisdictions in days — has now been picked up by mainland Chinese internet users. This is a rare, genuinely grassroots demonstration of civilian coordination across the Chinese-speaking world. 
The party-state has spent decades trying to make this impossible. Civil society organizations in China – independent labor unions, feminist and LBGTQ+ groups, rights-focused law firms, religious congregations, NGOs – have been systematically dismantled or captured. But, as Wang Wang’s case revealed, there is still the possibility for public action. Decentralized, apolitical interest communities of internet users come together over love of a shared subject – pets, in this case. When they feel wronged, they can mobilize.
Precisely because such expression is apolitical, it travels further inside China’s public sphere than any dissident message could. Shared life experience – grief for an animal, fury at cruelty, the moral compass of ordinary people – is among the few unifying forces the censorship system cannot easily counter.
That’s why the state now treats spontaneous compassion as a political threat, as the Shenyang notice showed. The authorities understand that autonomous grassroots coordination, on any subject, is dangerous.
The Pew Research Center reported this month that, for the first time in roughly 20 years of tracking, China is viewed more favorably than the United States in most countries surveyed (25 of 36). As official narratives compete, these citizen-funded billboards offer something neither Beijing’s propaganda nor Western commentary can: an unmediated look at what Chinese people themselves feel. A public that mourns a stray dog and demands the rule of law is a truer picture of China than any state broadcast, and a more humanizing one than any threat assessment.
How should democratic societies respond? Not with appropriation or instrumentalization – this movement belongs to the Chinese people. The right response is helping these stories be seen, so that the people who paid for a billboard in a city they will never visit can watch their message echo back.
Democratic municipalities and transit authorities could publish clear, content-neutral guidelines for public-interest advertising by overseas communities, so that approval does not depend on a facility manager’s private calculation of political risk. Crowdfunding platforms could build standing partnerships with outdoor-advertising companies to streamline compliant campaigns. None of this is China-specific; the same infrastructure would serve marginalized voices from anywhere whose domestic public square has been closed to them.
As a Hong Konger, I have seen firsthand the frightening speed with which a society can arrive at a place where a sign in your own window is a criminal risk. I also know what it means to people in those restricted circumstances to see their words appear on a screen in Times Square or on a building in Tokyo. That visibility is a sustaining force – proof to those inside that their voices carry. It’s also one of the few things that can preserve, and perhaps quietly foster, the civilian networks on which any future civic life in China will have to be built.
The boys who killed Wang Wang will face no trial. But the millions who refused to let her memory disappear have shown that Chinese civil society still lives.

articles.title: NATO-IP4 Relations Remain Stronger Than the Last Two Summits Suggest
articles.full_text:
Yes, the Indo-Pacific leaders were absent for the second year in a row. But that’s not because of a lack of interest in the partnership.
The chiefs of defense of the United States, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea attend a session on “Partners in the Indo-Pacific” at the 194th NATO Military Committee in Chiefs of Defense session in Brussels, Belgium, Jan. 22, 2026.
A notable feature of the July 2026 NATO Summit in Ankara was the absence, for the second year in a row, of the four leaders of NATO’s Indo-Pacific partner countries, collectively known as the IP4: Australia, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. It may be tempting to see this as evidence that NATO-IP4 relations are on the downturn, but a deeper analysis does not support such a conclusion. 
First, the main variable affecting the presence of the IP4 leaders was not the interest of NATO and IP4 countries in continued engagement, but the nature of the summits themselves. In addition, it is not clear that regular leader-level attendance at annual NATO summits is still a necessary driver of NATO-IP4 relations. The logic for continued cooperation between NATO and the IP4 is as strong as ever in the current geopolitical climate. 
Rather than the optics of NATO-IP4 relations, the underlying substance and direction of engagement, the subleader level institutionalization of these relationships, and their application at the practical level are the critical elements for gauging commitment. 
The key difference between the summits in 2022, 2023, and 2024 and the summits in 2025 and 2026 is in their structure. All three of those earlier summits involved two days of North Atlantic Council (NAC) meetings at leader level. The latter two summits had only one. Getting that attenuated timeline required cutting out the NAC leaders’ meetings with partner countries. 
That change in structure primarily reflects the realities of the United States. To paraphrase the words of an allied official, NATO understands that President Donald Trump does not have the interest or attention span for a two-day summit, so the summits had to be shortened – simply as a matter of practicality and realistic expectations. 
It is true that the IP4 leaders were still invited, and that most did not attend – that fact is indisputable. This decision becomes much more understandable when examined in context, however. Without an opportunity to take part in NAC discussions, the IP4 leaders were effectively invited to the rehearsal dinner, but not to the wedding itself. From the potential perspectives of busy heads of state, such an invitation simply does not carry the weight necessary to edge out competing domestic and regional priorities. It’s a nice opportunity, but – in combination with the simultaneous attendance of their defense ministers at complementary summit events for those peers – not a compelling one. 
It would be a mistake, however, to equate summit representation with the current health of the partner-alliance relationships. Leader attendance at the 2022, 2023, and 2024 summits, which each featured a NAC leader-level session with IP4 partners, was critical to moving NATO-IP4 relations forward, establishing their importance publicly, and creating the momentum from the top necessary to activate national bureaucracies. Those goals have now been met substantially, making continued leader-level attendance less vital. 
By 2024, all four of the partner countries had signed new Individually Tailored Partnership Program (ITPP) documents to map out their bilateral NATO relationships. They all had dedicated ambassadors to NATO at embassies in Belgium, and were engaged in specific NATO-IP4 priority areas of cooperation: Ukraine, cyber defense, disinformation, and technology.  
Certainly, leader-level attention is the best driver for continued internal momentum within each country and for the further deepening of these relationships. That said, top leaders’ absence from regular summit-based intervals could be offset, to a significant extent, by the greater involvement of defense and foreign ministers and the continued visits of high-level NATO officials to the region. There is a clear effort being made at NATO to create such opportunities and by IP4 partners to respond. 
The IP4 ministers of defense (minister of defense industry for Australia) attended the Ankara summit and met with their NATO counterparts at a NAC defense minister-level working dinner and a NATO defense industry forum, expanding on defense and foreign ministerial engagements from recent years. In 2025, new NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte traveled to Tokyo to meet with Japan’s prime minister and other high-level NATO officials visited the region, continuing a trend from the past few years. Perhaps most importantly, the NATO-IP4 relationships – bilaterally and as the IP4 – are already institutionalized at the ambassador and working levels in Brussels.
Geopolitical Drivers for Continued Engagement
There are at least four clear geopolitical drivers for continued engagement between NATO and its Indo-Pacific partners, based on mutual interests and benefit. These are the existence of related demands and expectations from the United States, the interconnected nature of security in the Indo-Pacific and Euro-Atlantic theaters and the prospect of multi-theater conflict, mutual support for a rules-based international system, and opportunities for defense industrial cooperation. In addition to the NATO-IP4 priority areas of cooperation agreed at the Washington Summit in 2024 (Ukraine, cyber defense, disinformation, and technology), and the ITPPs, these drivers create a clear basis for further relations. 
As countries that are all close U.S. allies (or in the case of New Zealand, a key partner), the IP4 and NATO nations can exchange best practices and views on the now more fragile U.S. alliance relationship, including by coordinating messaging and consulting on how to keep the United States engaged constructively beyond the Western Hemisphere and within recognized rules and norms on the use of force. In other words, there is a clear utility in having friends that are sharing similar experiences regarding their ally the United States, particularly as the U.S. president issues sets of connected demands and expectations for U.S. allies, regardless of location. This was evident mostly recently in Trump’s calls for increased regional burden-sharing and assistance with the Israeli-U.S. war against Iran. 
Mutually shared concerns about multi-theater conflict involving China and Russia also underscore the need to coordinate. As the war in Ukraine has made abundantly clear, security challenges in the Euro-Atlantic theater have significant, if indirect, security consequences for the Indo-Pacific theater and vice versa. The complications of inter-theater deterrence and defense dynamics have not gone away because the United States has shifted its attention away from Europe. Nor has the fear of coordinated multi-theater conflicts by China and Russia. 
Continuing strong relations between NATO and the IP4 is critical for thinking through together what would be necessary to prepare for and address simultaneous Chinese or North Korean and Russian led contingencies. The IP4 partners are also incorporating lessons from the Ukraine war into their own security assessments, with Japan – where the lessons of Ukraine are expected to feature prominently in the updated national security and defense documents expected later this year – as a prime example. 
Similarly, NATO and the IP4 share a desire to support a rules-based international system or critical parts of it. This is particularly true in areas where the partners can work well together, such as norm setting, public diplomacy, countering disinformation, coordination of political statements, and support for Ukraine. For the IP4 countries, along with many middle powers in Europe, security and prosperity has rested on a predictable, rules-based system. There is still an unwillingness to back away from that despite Russian, Chinese, and now U.S. propensities to undermine such a system. 
There is also the very practical issue of coordination on defense industrial cooperation. A number of potentially accessible avenues for such coordination between IP4 countries and NATO allies exist. Joint development and co-production of defense technologies and equipment is one. Here for example, NATO is reportedly in talks with the IP4 partners about participating in its Starlift project, an alliance network for sharing space satellite launch capabilities. Japan is also exploring access to NATO’s Defense Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA), focused on next-generation technologies. Japanese participation in DIANA could open new defense export opportunities in European markets now that Tokyo has further relaxed restrictions on arms exports.  
Another avenue is the diversification of defense-related supply chains, especially away from competitors and toward allies like Australia, Japan, or South Korea. A third is coordinating on munitions production and stockpiling, given that the shortfall in munitions has been a key lesson of the wars in Ukraine and now Iran. 
A fourth major avenue is greater interoperability through joint acquisition/procurement and the integration of technical standards across equipment/munitions. South Korea and NATO are in talks for a joint procurement agreement coming out of the Ankara Summit, for example. Australia signed an agreement with NATO’s Support and Procurement Organization in 2025. 
NATO’s interest in and engagement with its IP4 partners – and vice versa – continues, if simply less publicly.  That makes sense going forward, for the near term at least.  Now that the NATO-IP4 relationships have been established, normalized, and largely institutionalized, the focus should transition to maintaining regular engagement on important areas of mutual interest and to deepening through practical, substantive cooperation.

articles.title: The Power Behind Japan’s Takaichi Government
articles.full_text:
Nippon Ishin has, through its alliance with Takaichi, exerted an influence on the Japanese government that far exceeds its parliamentary strength.
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae (second from right) poses with Nippon Ishin leaders Yoshimura Hirofumi (second from left) and Fujita Fumitake (far right) on Feb. 9, 2026, a day after the LDP’s sweeping election victory.
On the day of a snap winter election – one that would ultimately end in a landslide victory for the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) – Takaichi  Sanae stood alongside two men. They were not members of her own party, but rather the two leaders of Nippon Ishin no Kai: Osaka Governor Yoshimura Hirofumi and Fujita Fumitake, who leads his party’s Diet delegation. Yet Yoshimura’s stump speech hardly sounded like one delivered by the leader of a different party. In fact, it barely sounded as though Takaichi herself belonged to the LDP.
“We may not have the numbers. But we will never back down. We will not leave Takaichi-san standing alone,” Yoshimura declared. “We will not let Japan stand alone. We are determined to move Japan forward. That is the resolve with which we stand here today.”
Before they joined the ruling coalition, Nippon Ishin’s initial favorite in the October 2025 LDP leadership race was Koizumi Shinjiro, now serving as minister of defense. They shared a commitment to challenging vested interests and embraced what are often described as “neoliberal” approaches to achieving that goal. By providing the LDP with enough votes to secure a parliamentary majority – which it lacked in both houses at the time – Nippon Ishin hoped to advance a reform agenda that would have been impossible to pursue as a mid-sized opposition party alone. 
Although Yoshimura never explicitly endorsed a preferred successor to Ishiba Shigeru, his description of Koizumi as a “politician who embodies the spirit of reform” and “a true reformer” left little doubt about his own – and his party’s – preferred candidate. Consequently, Takaichi’s victory came as a shock to Nippon Ishin. The party had not only expected Koizumi to prevail but also lacked close political ties to Takaichi and her inner circle.
However, the events that unfolded after Takaichi’s election opened a window that had long been thought closed. The LDP’s longtime coalition partner, Komeito, declined to form a government under her leadership, citing frustration with the LDP’s handling of the political funding scandal and doubts that the reforms Komeito sought would be implemented on its preferred timetable. As a result, the once-automatic path from LDP president to Japanese prime minister was no longer assured. The former members of the Democratic Party of Japan were seeking to reassemble. During the ensuing political deadlock, Takaichi wryly referred to herself as “the woman who may never become prime minister.”
Then came Nippon Ishin to the rescue. With the help of  Takashi Endo of Nippon Ishin – who is well known for his cross-party connections and served as an intermediary between Yoshimura and Takaichi – Yoshimura came to see Takaichi as a fellow reformer, while Takaichi, in turn, came to believe that they had more in common than she had initially thought. The coalition talks gained speed, and a week after the leaders talked, there was a coalition agreement. 
Since becoming prime minister, Takaichi has begun implementing key elements of the coalition agreement, many of which had already been on her own policy agenda for years and were included in her campaign platform during the February election. One example is the bill criminalizing the desecration of the Japanese flag – a measure she unsuccessfully sought to enact in both 2012 and 2021. 
Likewise, the security reforms now underway reflect a longstanding agenda of LDP conservatives, including Takaichi, who had long argued that Komeito constrained their ambitions. With Nippon Ishin replacing Komeito as the LDP’s coalition partner, those constraints have largely disappeared. Although the coalition agreement was not exclusively focused on security, it was disproportionately heavy on that area, enabling the LDP’s conservative wing to pursue long-sought defense and public security reforms. 
At the same time, Takaichi’s political indebtedness to Nippon Ishin is widely cited as a reason her government has embraced policies that were not previously among her priorities. The extent of that indebtedness was evident when she introduced legislation to reduce the number of seats in the House of Representatives by 10 percent, explaining that the proposal was a promise the LDP made to Nippon Ishin. The measure provoked fierce opposition, particularly from parties that rely heavily on proportional representation, where most of the proposed seat reductions would have occurred, prompting them to boycott Diet deliberations. 
Although Takaichi ultimately withdrew the bill after consulting Yoshimura, her willingness to press ahead with such a politically contentious proposal underscored the extent to which she felt compelled to accommodate her new coalition partner. Despite Nippon Ishin lacking the electoral machine that Komeito had, Takaichi seems not to have forgotten the helping hand her new partner extended to her.
Some observers have described Nippon Ishin as “Takaichi’s faction,” suggesting that it has effectively become her political power base outside the LDP. The characterization aptly captures Takaichi’s position within her own party. Long regarded as an outsider within the LDP, she reached the pinnacle of power not by cultivating the support of party elders, but by building a strong following among the conservative grassroots and forging a close political alliance with late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo, the party’s leading conservative figure. Her decision to call a snap election in early 2026 was partly motivated by a desire to consolidate her grip on a party that still included many moderates and fiscal conservatives who remained skeptical of her social conservatism and support for expansionary fiscal policy.
At least, that was how Nippon Ishin appeared to interpret it. While campaigning during the snap election, Nippon Ishin Secretary General Hiroshi Nakatsukasa argued that “there are still forces of resistance within the LDP,” adding, “Our job is to keep a close watch on that. We will support the prime minister, keep politics moving forward, and serve as the accelerator for the government.” The remarks underscored the party’s self-perception as both Takaichi’s protector against resistance within the LDP (“We will not leave Takaichi-san standing alone”) and the driving force behind her reform agenda (“We are determined to move Japan forward”).
There are growing calls within the LDP to reconsider the coalition with Nippon Ishin now that the party enjoys a supermajority on its own, with some arguing that Nippon Ishin’s neoliberal agenda has become more of a nuisance than an asset. Yet for a party founded on the principle of decentralizing Japan’s governing apparatus, the passage of the deputy capital bill represents a significant achievement, and the fact that the LDP extended the Diet session just for that purpose attests to Takaichi’s resolve to pay back her debt. 
Takaichi and the LDP’s defense hawks may increasingly come to view Nippon Ishin as an external catalyst capable of nudging the party further to the right on constitutional revision and a more forward-leaning nuclear policy, including support for nuclear-sharing arrangements with the United States.
The differences between the two parties are perhaps most evident in the Diet’s Commission on the Constitution, the parliamentary committee responsible for deliberating constitutional amendments. While the LDP seeks to preserve the existing wording of Article 9, Paragraph 2 – which renounces the maintenance of “war potential” – Nippon Ishin advocates deleting Paragraph 2 altogether and replacing the Self-Defense Forces with a constitutionally recognized National Defense Force. 
More broadly, the debate over Japan’s defense posture highlights the divide between Takaichi and her intra-party rivals. Whereas her opponents have generally preferred a more incremental approach to constitutional reform and defense policy, Takaichi’s strengthened position – further reinforced by cooperation with Nippon Ishin – has left them with little room to publicly challenge her agenda.
Although Nippon Ishin may increasingly find itself marginalized by the LDP’s overwhelming parliamentary majority, and several of its signature policy goals – including a ban on corporate and organizational political donations and sweeping social security reform – remain in limbo, many of its priorities, particularly in the areas of national security, are being incorporated into government policy. The measure provoked fierce opposition, particularly from parties that rely heavily on proportional representation, where most of the proposed seat reductions would have occurred, prompting them to boycott Diet deliberations. 
Although Takaichi ultimately withdrew the bill after consulting Yoshimura, her willingness to press ahead with such a politically contentious proposal underscored the extent to which she felt compelled to accommodate her new coalition partner. Despite Nippon Ishin lacking the electoral machine that Komeito had, Takaichi seems not to have forgotten the helping hand her new partner extended to her.
Some observers have described Nippon Ishin as “Takaichi’s faction,” suggesting that it has effectively become her political power base outside the LDP. The characterization aptly captures Takaichi’s position within her own party. Long regarded as an outsider within the LDP, she reached the pinnacle of power not by cultivating the support of party elders, but by building a strong following among the conservative grassroots and forging a close political alliance with late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo, the party’s leading conservative figure. Her decision to call a snap election in early 2026 was partly motivated by a desire to consolidate her grip on a party that still included many moderates and fiscal conservatives who remained skeptical of her social conservatism and support for expansionary fiscal policy.
articles.summary: Nippon Ishin has, through its alliance with Takaichi, exerted an influence on the Japanese government that far exceeds its parliamentary strength.

articles.title: The Rise of North Korea’s Nuclear-Armed Navy
articles.full_text:
North Korea has modified its hierarchy of defense priorities by elevating the importance of the KPAN.
This photo, provided by North Korean state media, shows the Choe Hyon destroyer on the occasion of the ship’s commissioning, June 23, 2026.
Nuclear-capable cruise missiles rose from the soon-to-be commissioned North Korean guided missile destroyer, Kang Kon (52), as Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un watched on July 3. The launch was conducted less than two weeks after the Korean People’s Army Navy (KPAN) formally commissioned the 5,000-ton destroyer Choe Hyon (51), North Korea’s largest domestically produced surface warship. 
These two events underscore indications that North Korea is engaging in a concerted effort to build up its navy. At the Choe Hyon’s commissioning, Kim declared that the KPAN had entered a “new era” after “over 70 years” of naval stagnation.
These developments indicate that North Korea has modified its hierarchy of defense priorities by elevating the importance of the KPAN. The rapid construction of large surface combatants, new naval bases, and modernization of existing bases are evidence of this elevation. If continued, this trend could disrupt allied naval dominance and complicate U.S. nuclear deterrence efforts. That, in turn, could encourage the Kim regime to act more aggressively, increasing the probability of a conflict breaking out on the Korean Peninsula. Fortunately, the United States, South Korea, and Japan can still counter this developing threat. 
Comparing the troubled history of North Korea’s navy in the 2010s with more recent developments provides evidence of the growing threat and insights into how to respond.
North Korea’s focus on naval development can be traced back to 2023 when Kim signaled his desire for greater emphasis on KPAN growth and modernization to increase its involvement in military strategy and operations. Three years later, in February 2026 at the 9th Congress of the Workers’ Party of Korea, Kim unveiled his new five-year plan and future defense priorities. 
The five-year plan calls for upgrading all military bases, further strengthening the southern border, and modernizing conventional weapons so that they may become “world-class.” In March, Kim stated that the KPAN needs to build two vessels of a size equivalent to the Choe Hyon or larger every year, with the goal being at least 12 large surface combatants by the early 2030s. 
These goals further expanded in June 2026 when Kim directed his regime to accelerate the design and construction of a new 10,000-ton guided missile cruiser and build additional naval bases. Concurrently, the North appears to be expanding shipyards at Chongjin and Nampho to better facilitate Kim’s yearly shipbuilding quota.
If the gains in basing and industrial production are realized, sustained, and institutionalized, Pyongyang may be able to sustain the current pace of surface combatant production. Fielding a formidable surface combatant force could undermine U.S. and South Korean sea control around the Korean Peninsula. It would also be a significant break from the past, when the KPAN struggled to build and field even smaller vessels.
Before the shift toward large naval surface combatants and the subsequent commissioning of the Choe Hyon in June 2026, the KPAN was focused on building, outfitting, and commissioning two different classes of corvettes. The most capable were the two vessels of the Amnok class. Displacing around 2,000 tons, those two vessels feature a reduced radar cross section, and at least one’s armament includes a 100mm main gun, anti-submarine warfare rocket launchers on the bow, missile launchers for anti-air missiles and possibly anti-ship missiles, and a close-in weapon system (CIWS) similar to the Soviet AK-630. 
Patrol Ship No. 661, the only publicly seen Amnok-class corvette, made its debut in state media in August 2023. Naval News reported at the time that most weapons and sensors onboard were “severely” obsolete in comparison with Western and other Asian designs. However, the vessel marked a major milestone for the KPAN as No. 661 was, at the time, one of its most capable ships.
Around the same time, Pyongyang built and fielded two other corvettes of the significantly less capable Tuman class. They lack extensive armament and are posited by some analysts to serve in a support role for the more capable Amnok-class vessels.
Despite the capability differences between the Amnok and Tuman classes, both suffered from lengthy construction and outfitting timelines, along with apparent setbacks. For instance, No. 661 was first spotted under construction in 2011, entered service in 2017, and finally had its capabilities debut in August 2023. It seemingly took more than a decade for the ship to undergo construction, outfitting, and sea trials. 
Tuman-class vessels also suffered from long completion timelines, with initial construction beginning in 2011 and completing in 2013. But then reconstruction of one vessel started in 2014, with reconstruction of the other starting in 2017, indicating significant issues with initial design, construction, or weapons loadout. Despite no state media announcement that either Tuman-class vessel entered service, reporting indicates at least one is likely on the active register. 
The troubled history of these ships contrasts sharply with the much more successful development of the Choe Hyon-class destroyers.
The Choe Hyon’s construction efforts began around February 2024 at Nampho shipyard on North Korea’s western coast. It was launched successfully in April 2025 and sea trials began afterward. The final testing of seaworthiness appeared to occur in May 2026, while its eventual commissioning was on June 23, 2026 — less than two and a half years after construction started.
The increased speed of construction is alarming, as are the Choe Hyon’s combat capabilities. After undergoing modifications throughout 2025 and possibly into early 2026, the vessel’s primary weapon system is now a mixture of 88 large, medium, and small diameter vertical launch system (VLS) cells that can fire cruise and surface-to-air missiles. The Kim regime regularly touts the ability of the vessel to launch “strategic” nuclear-tipped cruise missiles. If this is true, the Choe Hyon provides yet another vector, in addition to ground-launched and submarine-launched missiles, by which North Korea can threaten U.S., South Korean, and Japanese military bases and regional cities with nuclear weapons. 
The Choe Hyon also fields a 127mm main gun on the bow, torpedo launchers, decoy-launching systems, and two CIWS that resemble Chinese Type 730 rotary cannons, likely guided by the installed four-faced phased array radars or an integrated fire-control radar. Additionally, it is armed with eight inclined launchers concealed within the central superstructure amidships as well as eight ready-to-fire short-range missiles on an apparatus which closely resembles the Russian Pantsir-M CIWS. 
The Choe Hyon could have protection against higher velocity threats, such as some anti-ship missiles, via the Pantsir-M’s 57E6M-E missiles if truly armed with a Pantsir-M or a close derivative. That would also indicate that Pyongyang’s relationship with Moscow has provided tangible defense benefits. If the technology underlying the Choe Hyon’s CIWS came from Chinese and Russian-exported systems, then Beijing and Moscow could be providing the terminal layer of defense for an arm of Pyongyang’s nuclear weapons capabilities. These CIWS could potentially disrupt American, South Korean, or Japanese efforts to prevent a North Korean nuclear launch – a threat will be further amplified as more vessels in this class enter active service.
Pyongyang’s already robust and rapidly growing relationship with Moscow is a part of a larger web of security cooperation among the “axis of aggressors” – China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. This cooperation is unlikely to end anytime soon and brings significant benefits to its members, as detailed in a new book by Bradley Bowman, Elaine Dezenski, and RADM (ret.) Mark Montgomery.
The second Choe Hyon-class vessel, the Kang Kon, was launched unsuccessfully in May 2025 as Kim Jong Un watched. Satellite imagery revealed that a side launch was attempted, as opposed to the Choe Hyon’s drydock launch method. When a ship is launched via drydock, the chamber where the ship was constructed is flooded with water, floating the ship in a controlled manner. A side launch is a riskier process whereby a ship is constructed on land and then is slid into the water on its side via oiled slideways. 
The change from the Choe Hyon’s drydock launch and the Kang Kon’s side launch was possibly due to differences between the facilities at Chongjin and Nampho, where the Choe Hyon was launched. A lack of relevant experience with side launches and a rush to finish the project may have also contributed to the Kang Kon ending up with its starboard side facing the bottom and a portion of its bow remaining on the slipway.
In a rare moment of candor by North Korean state media, the accident was quickly announced, and “inexperienced command and operational carelessness” were given as the underlying reasons for the mishap. State media further revealed that the hull was damaged via “low-impact holes” at the bow section during the accident.
However, the accident would prove to be a relatively minor setback. The Kang Kon was quickly raised and towed to another shipyard at Rajin, further northeast. From there, on June 12, 2025, the KPAN ceremoniously “relaunched” the ship. It took North Korea only around 22 days to raise the ship, relaunch it, and begin sea trials. While it is unclear if the Kang Kon fielded its full complement of weapon systems at that time, it is clear the construction timeline remained short despite the accident.
The KPAN built and fielded their largest-ever naval surface combatant in a little over two years and will likely come close to that feat again, with the Kang Kon expected to be commissioned in 2026 or early 2027. North Korea has now produced roughly 5,000-ton destroyers faster than it used to produce 2,000-ton corvettes, with two more destroyers of the same size currently under construction. Furthermore, the destroyers have modern combat capabilities in their VLS cells that make them a serious conventional and nuclear threat to U.S., South Korean, and Japanese forces. 
The KPAN’s increasing combat capabilities will potentially complicate U.S., South Korean, and Japanese defense planning related to sea control and nuclear deterrence, at a minimum. These challenges will only grow if the KPAN is able to overcome the remaining hurdles of integrating modern technology into command-and-control suites, enhancing the training of sailors, further expanding shipbuilding capacity, and adopting modern naval combat tactics.
Washington, Seoul, and Tokyo should recognize the growing threat and deepen trilateral cooperation to counter it. Those efforts should involve regular trilateral military exercises that include not just naval and air assets but also ground forces and integrated command structures. Washington should also maintain a robust U.S. military force posture in South Korea, signaling its political will and military capability to punish and defeat aggression. 
At the political level, President Donald Trump should convene without delay a summit with his Japanese and South Korean counterparts to highlight and strengthen efforts to deepen trilateral security cooperation, building on the successful 2023 summit. This effort should also produce a new trilateral strategy to deter North Korean aggression and counter the dangerous partnership between Pyongyang and Moscow. 
Additionally, the U.S. Congress should require the Department of Defense to publish a previously congressionally mandated report – a requirement that expired in 2017 – on North Korean military capabilities that includes the regime’s growing security cooperation with Russia and China. Congress should also require reports on whether U.S. military capabilities and war plans on the peninsula account for growing North Korean capabilities and impose additional sanctions on Russia over its security cooperation with North Korea.
articles.summary: North Korea has modified its hierarchy of defense priorities by elevating the importance of the KPAN.

articles.title: Born in Jails, Popularized by Gandhi, Hunger Strikes Can Hit Authorities Hard. Conditions Apply.
articles.full_text:
Sonam Wangchuk has ended his 26-day hunger strike supporting the Cockroach Janta Party’s demand for the education minister’s resignation. What did it achieve?
Social activist Sonam Wangchuk (right) ends his 26-day-long hunger strike after reaching an agreement with the Narendra Modi government, New Delhi, India, July 24, 2026.
Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk’s 26-day fast, which he ended on Thursday night, has not yet achieved the protestors’ goal: the sacking of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. But it has created impact; it has put the Narendra Modi government on the back foot for the first time since the farmers’ protests in 2021.
Wangchuk’s decision to end the hunger strike came after the government moved to address the NEET paper leak controversy and youth protests with a series of assurances. Thousands of students and youth protesters are still occupying the Jantar Mantar area in New Delhi.
Following Wangchuk’s decision to end the fast, Abhijit Dipke – the founder of India’s satirical political movement, the Cockroach Janta Party – expressed relief, saying that Wangchuk’s life is precious. He vowed that the movement will continue until Pradhan resigns or is sacked. “We won’t let Wangchuk’s immense sacrifice go in vain,” Dipke said.
The hunger strike as a mode of protest and resistance in the modern era is believed to have originated in Tsarist Russia in the late 19th century when prisoners refused food, seeking an end to inhumane treatment. Later, in the U.K. and the U.S., women’s suffrage activists in prison used hunger strikes to seek “political prisoner” status. In both countries, the prison authorities’ attempts to force-feed the hunger strikers triggered adverse sentiments and ultimately helped mobilization of public opinion in favor of the protesters.
In Ireland, independence activists also used it in jails to galvanize support for better prison conditions and the cause of independence. Irish prisoner Bobby Sands’ death after refusing food for 66 days triggered public sympathy for his cause.
In India, Mohandas “Mahatma” Gandhi brought this mode of protest into the public sphere — outside prison walls — starting with a fast in support of workers’ demand for a wage hike in 1918. He succeeded in making the mill owners concede his demands.
Thereafter, Gandhi used hunger strikes quite successfully to unite a large and diverse population against the British colonial powers as peacefully as possible — not only until India’s independence in 1947, but also after, especially to stop communal riots.
Gandhi was not alone in using this form of protest. During the independence movement, militant activists Bhagat Singh and Jatin Das, among many others, went on hunger strike during their prison days. Das’ death triggered nationwide protests and increased support for the independence movement. Gandhi, nevertheless, was the one to use it effectively outside the jail premises — where he had many other modes of protest available. His extraordinary success gave this mode of protest global popularity in the decades that followed.
It remained popular in independent India too, with some notable achievements and some despairing failures.
Potti Sriramulu’s 58-day fast for a Telugu-speaking state in 1952 ended with his death. But the public sentiment it generated led to the achievement of the demand — the creation of Andhra State in 1953. Six decades later, K. Chandrasekhar Rao’s fast‑unto‑death in 2009 accelerated the creation of a separate Telangana state, carved out of Andhra Pradesh.
However, Manipuri activist Irom Sharmila’s 16-year hunger strike failed to achieve her objective. Even though the fast drew attention to the draconian provisions of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, the law was not repealed. She was force-fed through a tube in her nose in a hospital in government custody until she broke her fast to return to normal life in 2016. She said she hadn’t achieved anything through her prolonged fasting. She contested an election but was defeated.
A history of hunger strikes shows that they create a larger impact only when their cause strikes a chord with a large population’s direct and immediate interest, the demands are narrow and meetable, and the hunger-striker enjoys some sort of pre-existing authority or reputation and draws support from organized political or civil society movements. The nature of the adversary also plays a role in the success of such a mode of protest.
In 2018, scientist-turned-ascetic Guru Das Agrawal, one of India’s leading environmentalists, died following a 111-day fast seeking government promise and action for saving the Ganges River from pollution. The media showed little interest in his fast until he died. The government did not care either.
Wangchuk began his indefinite hunger strike in New Delhi on June 28. It gained larger public attention only from July 16-17, when it was reported that he had lost over 9 kilograms of weight due to fasting.
Several factors worked in drawing public attention and sympathy. The first was that the cause – exam system reforms and the demand for the education minister’s removal – had already become a major concern. The second was that Wangchuk had been in the media spotlight for some time. A Ramon Magsaysay awardee, he has a history of activism, including one that cost him 170 days in detention for his participation in the Ladakh protests last year. Third, leftist student groups lent their support at the recent hunger strike venue in New Delhi.
Besides, he has enjoyed a sort of celebrity image, partly due to the public perception that a prominent character in a Bollywood blockbuster was based on him.
During 2011-13, social activist Anna Hazare’s fasts in Delhi played a key role in galvanizing public opinion against the then Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government. Hazare was well-known in his home state of Maharashtra but was not as eminent as Wangchuk is nationwide. However, the crowd that gathered around Hazare included some big names: former top cop Kiran Bedi, lawyer Prashant Bhushan, and rights activist Medha Patkar, among others.
Besides, the image of a frail old man in Gandhian attire launching a hunger strike seeking measures to prevent corruption when the UPA government was rocked by a series of scam charges struck a chord with many people across the country.
Importantly, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) was stage-managing the event, which culminated in the fall of the UPA government in 2014.
This is one of the reasons why the Congress, India’s main opposition party, has been skeptical about Wangchuk and the CJP. Are they mere fronts for someone else?
Despite the doubts and suspicions, the Congress entered the scene after police forcefully took Wangchuk to hospital, a CJP-called protest march early this week drew massive crowds, and clashes broke out between cops and the protesters.
Wangchuk has ended his fast. But the momentum that it has generated may not be lost too soon.
“Our protest has now reached another level, and we will not stop. Everyone wants only one thing-Dharmendra Pradhan Must Resign!” Dipke said on Friday.
Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk’s 26-day fast, which he ended on Thursday night, has not yet achieved the protestors’ goal: the sacking of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. But it has created impact; it has put the Narendra Modi government on the back foot for the first time since the farmers’ protests in 2021.
Wangchuk’s decision to end the hunger strike came after the government moved to address the NEET paper leak controversy and youth protests with a series of assurances. Thousands of students and youth protesters are still occupying the Jantar Mantar area in New Delhi.
Following Wangchuk’s decision to end the fast, Abhijit Dipke – the founder of India’s satirical political movement, the Cockroach Janta Party – expressed relief, saying that Wangchuk’s life is precious. He vowed that the movement will continue until Pradhan resigns or is sacked. “We won’t let Wangchuk’s immense sacrifice go in vain,” Dipke said.

In both countries, the prison authorities’ attempts to force-feed the hunger strikers triggered adverse sentiments and ultimately helped mobilization of public opinion in favor of the protesters.
In Ireland, independence activists also used it in jails to galvanize support for better prison conditions and the cause of independence. Irish prisoner Bobby Sands’ death after refusing food for 66 days triggered public sympathy for his cause.

articles.title: Jakarta, the Sinking Metropolis Where Millions Still Struggle to Access Piped Water
articles.full_text:
Excessive groundwater extraction by households and industry is one of the primary reasons for the city’s subsidence.
Thousands of families in Penjaringan, North Jakarta, rely on expensive deliveries from water trucks.
The blue water tanker rumbles into the narrow lanes of Muara Angke, a fishing community on Jakarta’s northern coast, every few days.
Within minutes, residents emerge carrying hoses and plastic containers. Some connect pipes snaking through the densely packed community. Others wait with buckets.
For families here, in one of the poorest neighborhoods in the world’s most populous metropolis, the truck delivers something millions of people in Indonesia’s capital still cannot rely on: clean water.
“When the deliveries stop, life quickly becomes impossible,” said Ellah, who runs a small neighborhood water kiosk.
“For seven days,” she recalled of one such instance, “people couldn’t wash. They couldn’t cook.”
Jakarta’s public water utility, PAM JAYA, says it is trying to change that.
Since returning the city’s water system to full public control in 2023, the utility has embarked on its most ambitious expansion in decades, aiming to provide piped water to every household by 2029.
It says coverage has already increased from just over 60 percent, when it took over, to about 82 percent of residents this year, with tens of thousands of new household connections installed over the past year as part of a broader effort to reduce dependence on groundwater.
But it is more than just about ensuring access to clean water.
Home to more than 12 million people in the city proper and 42 million in the wider metropolitan area, Jakarta is also globally known as the world’s fastest-sinking city – one of the prime reasons behind the controversial decision to build a new capital, Nusantara, in East Kalimantan.
Scientists say excessive groundwater extraction in Jakarta, rather than rising sea levels, is the primary reason parts of the city are sinking by up to 15 centimeters a year, with some studies recording even faster rates. Some neighborhoods have already subsided by as much as four meters since the 1970s.
Reliable piped water is widely regarded as one of the most important long-term solutions. The more households connected to the network, the fewer need to drill wells into the aquifers beneath the city.
Yet for millions of Jakartans, that transition remains incomplete.
Unlike much of the city, municipal pipes have never reached Ellah’s community of about 200 families living in wooden homes above the tidal waters of the north coast.
So in 2016, she built her own miniature distribution system.
Every few days, she buys an 8,000-liter tanker of water, stores it in large tanks outside her home, and sells it to around 15 neighboring households through a web of plastic hoses.
For many families, buying enough water for cooking, washing, and bathing can cost up to 600,000 rupiah ($33) a month. Average monthly household salaries in the area are about 1.5 to 3 million rupiah ($80 to $160).
“We feel like we are just ignored out here on the sides [of the city],” Ellah said.
Nearby, 68-year-old former fisherman Husnin also buys water instead of receiving it through household pipes.
His family spends around 40,000 rupiah ($2.20) every three days on water for washing and cooking, while drinking water must be purchased separately from refill stations.
Those costs have become harder to absorb as fish stocks decline and incomes shrink.
“[Access to water] is our right as citizens,” he said. “And it is the responsibility of the government to provide it.”
Nearby in Penjaringan, 46-year-old grandmother Sadiya has no piped connection either.
Instead, a hose runs from a nearby mosque, where groundwater is pumped into her home for 150,000 rupiah each month.
When the pump fails, she must buy water from vendors, spending as much as 30,000 rupiah a day ($1.70) – a huge burden for a household that sometimes earns less than 1 million rupiah ($56) each month.
“I feel sad,” she said. “Sometimes I’m late on the monthly payment because the money has to be divided for everything else.”
Meanwhile, just a few kilometers away in Rawabadan Selatan, families were connected to the municipal water network about two years ago. They had previously relied on bore water, which, due to seawater infiltration and pollution, was often too dirty to cook, bathe, and even clean with.
“It is so much better,” said Walimah of the piped supply.  “Previously [the borehole water] made us itchy. We had to rinse again with [cleaner] water.”
articles.summary: Excessive groundwater extraction by households and industry is one of the primary reasons for the city's subsidence.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Readmission to ASEAN Summits Still ‘Far Off,’ Special Envoy Says
articles.full_text:
Ma. Theresa Lazaro said that the bloc wants to see more progress on the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus for resolving the country’s conflict.
The return of Myanmar’s leaders to top meetings of the Association of Southeast ​Asian Nations (ASEAN) remains “far off,” the bloc’s special envoy said yesterday, despite the efforts of the country’s new military-backed civilian government to gain readmission.
Speaking at a press conference after an ASEAN meeting in Manila, Reuters reported, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said that Myanmar’s compliance with ASEAN’s ​Five-Point Consensus plan for resolving the conflict was still ​being assessed.
“It’s still far off,” said ​Lazaro, who is serving as ASEAN’s special envoy on Myanmar this year, while the Philippines holds the bloc’s rotating chairmanship. “There ​have been a lot of questions on their compliance.”
She added that ASEAN plans to come up with benchmarks to measure progress on the implementation of the Consensus, and that “failure to meet those would constitute non-compliance,” Reuters paraphrased her as saying.
“It’s still the Five-Point Consensus that is still being the foundational document that we are looking at during the discussions with the foreign minister of Myanmar,” Lazaro added.
The Five-Point Consensus was formulated by ASEAN in April 2021, two months after the coup that threw the country into political and economic turmoil. As well as recommending the appointment of a special envoy, it called for an immediate cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to Myanmar’s conflict.
Despite agreeing to the Consensus, coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has since done little to implement its most important points, instead choosing to defeat by force the groups opposing military rule, which his regime has characterized as “terrorists.” This lack of compliance led ASEAN to bar the military’s representatives from its summits in late 2021.
Since being anointed president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has pushed hard to normalize Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN – but has shown no more interest in implementing the terms of the Five-Point Consensus. Earlier this month, Myanmar’s pro-military parliament adopted a motion rejecting the Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, and that it “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.”
Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a press statement yesterday, arguing that the Five-Point Consensus “was attached as an annex” to a statement by the ASEAN chair, “without prior notification and circulation of a draft” to Myanmar. It was therefore “released without reaching a consensus among all Member States.” (For this reason, the Ministry referred to the ASEAN plan as the “Five-Point Statement.”)
The statement added that the government was “obliged to respect” the motion passed by its parliament – a message that it said Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe conveyed to his ASEAN colleagues when he met them for an “informal meeting” in Bangkok on July 12.
It said that in the discussion and implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, ASEAN member states “should respect and uphold ASEAN’s fundamental principles,” such as “respect for the sovereignty of Member States and non-interference in internal affairs.”
The curious thing about the current impasse is that Myanmar has grown more obdurate and defiant, right at the moment that ASEAN showed signs of adopting a more flexible policy toward Myanmar. Thailand, in particular, has pushed hard to bring Myanmar back into the “ASEAN family,” as its Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkaew put it in February. Sihasak helped broker the July 12 meeting in Bangkok, the first face-to-face meeting with the Myanmar foreign minister since the coup, a move that was criticized by human rights organizations and Myanmar opposition groups.
Lazaro’s comments suggest that even though ASEAN is seemingly trending toward the reintegration of Myanmar, this is unlikely without some significant gestures of compliance with the Five-Point Consensus. Lazaro is planning to lead a mission to Myanmar later in the year.
