Lazaro’s comments suggest that even though ASEAN is seemingly trending toward the reintegration of Myanmar, this is unlikely without some significant gestures of compliance with the Five-Point Consensus. Lazaro is planning to lead a mission to Myanmar later in the year.
The return of Myanmar’s leaders to top meetings of the Association of Southeast ​Asian Nations (ASEAN) remains “far off,” the bloc’s special envoy said yesterday, despite the efforts of the country’s new military-backed civilian government to gain readmission.
Speaking at a press conference after an ASEAN meeting in Manila, Reuters reported, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said that Myanmar’s compliance with ASEAN’s ​Five-Point Consensus plan for resolving the conflict was still ​being assessed.
Sebastian Strangio is Southeast Asia editor at The Diplomat.
articles.summary: Ma. Theresa Lazaro said that the bloc wants to see more progress on the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus for resolving the country's conflict.

articles.title: Squabble Deepens Between People Power Party’s Current and Former Leaders
articles.full_text:
Whether Han Dong-hoon and Jang Dong-hyuk mend ties will determine the future of South Korea’s main conservative party.
Han Dong-hoon speaks at a briefing session for parents of students taking the university admission exam, July 12, 2026.
On June 3, Han Dong-hoon, former leader of the opposition People Power Party (PPP), miraculously won the parliamentary by-election to represent a northern district in Busan. A couple of days later, amid his supporters’ cheers and camera flicks, he lingered before the granite steps leading up to the National Assembly. For a second he looked relieved, but the resolute look that immediately followed indicated what a slog lay ahead for him. 
Back in January, the PPP kicked Han out over allegations that the former party leader mobilized his family to slander former President Yoon Suk-yeol and his wife online. But in reality, it was more because Jang Dong-hyuk, the new PPP leader and a staunch Yoon supporter, didn’t want to see Han stirring up intra-party dissent over his leadership. 
Han led the PPP from December 2023 to April 2024 and then again from July to December 2024. During his leadership, Han locked horns with Yoon and openly defied Yoon’s martial law declaration and failed self-coup in December 2024.
The PPP leadership has come to blame Han for the Yoon administration’s – and the party’s – demise. They believe that Han’s open clashes with Yoon were to blame for the rout in the April 2024 general elections that earned the liberal bloc almost a two-third parliamentary majority. In reality, had it not been for Han’s sensible critique of the Yoon administration, the PPP would have lost more parliamentary seats. 
Han critics also believe that Yoon’s impeachment motion was passed in December 2024 largely due to pro-Han legislators joining the liberal camp in voting in favor. 
Han is now testing the waters to get back into the PPP. The prevailing mood within the party is one of awed recognition of his election victory. He competed against strong candidates from the ruling Democratic Party (DP) and the PPP. Given how the right-wing votes were split between Han and the PPP, his win was quite an achievement. One PPP legislator said Han was like “a star” with “power of absorption.”
Han began his courting, too, joining forums and sub-groups headed by the PPP grandees. Some PPP big shots not chummy with Han even co-signed Han’s amendment bill. Although they may have had an ulterior motive of embracing Han to siphon pro-Han votes in future elections, this could provide a secure foothold for Han to enter the PPP again. 
Not surprisingly, though, Jang is all frowns. “I’m sure that admitting Han into the PPP will be of no help in terms of the party expansion, solidarity and consolidation,” Jang said categorically on July 21. 
There have been some voices within the party calling for Jang to resign to take responsibility for the dismal June local elections results. Instead, Jang has come under flak for keeping his ears shut against criticism and staging solo activities outside the parliament. 
Of late, he has been frequenting – by himself – Seoul Olympic Park, where hundreds of demonstrators are demanding justice and accountability for how the Election Commission fielded fewer ballots than the number of registered voters. During the June local elections, as a result, dozens of constituents were turned away at some polling stations, having been denied the right to vote. 
This is an egregious institutional wrong and failure, and the PPP’s official stance is to file election petitions for investigation and partial re-election in the areas where the voters couldn’t exercise their democratic right. However, Jang is insisting on a complete re-run of the June local elections. This is not only infeasible but also represents Jang’s pandering to the far-right election fraud conspiracy that deems every election to have been rigged.
But Jang is stubborn. “He always says ‘I am right,’ ‘I am isolated’ and ‘I am aggrieved,’” said one PPP legislator, describing Jang’s refusal to listen to others. “Acting alone doesn’t mean leadership. A leader should be moving all 110 PPP legislators together,” said another PPP lawmaker. 
Cho Gab-je, perhaps the most respected conservative commentator and former head of the monthly magazine of Chosun Ilbo, South Korea’s largest conservative daily, chipped in in favor of Han. “Han is better than all the 110 PPP legislators combined,” he said. “Han’s diction and prose are armed with the constitution, facts and common sense,” Cho added. 
Meanwhile, Cho opined that “Jang is acting cute with his far-right supporters” and picking fights with Han to prolong his political life. 
On the other hand, Han is keeping cool. “I look forward to rebuilding conservatism and taking back the administration in 2030, not the past,” Han said. He isn’t alone. While Jang insists on further consolidating the PPP’s registered members, Jeong Jeom-sig, the PPP floor leader, said on July 20 that “we can’t just operate with just our members and their wishes,” pointing out that the party should really be “people’s party.” 
In that sense, he’s more open to the idea – and the necessity, really – of letting Han back into the PPP fold. Jeong said hs is hoping for a “consensus” from “many people” – including, but apparently not limited to, the PPP members and legislators.
Oh Se-hoon, Seoul’s new mayor and one of the few PPP candidates to emerge victorious in the local elections, went even further. He had already scuffled with Jang over the direction, or the lack thereof, of intra-party reform ahead of the June local elections. Now, Oh is calling for abolishing the PPP chairship. “Do we really need a party chairperson?” he asked in one forum in late June as a calculated jab at Jang. Recently, he has been dining with influential PPP legislators, including the floor leader Jeong, to discuss how to reform the party. 
Jang’s leadership, however, seems safe for now. According to a major pollster, the PPP’s approval ratings bounded up into the 40 percent range in mid-July. PPP supporters seem to have momentarily coalesced to give their party a chance to stitch up their differences and fight the DP on major fronts, including what to do with the Election Commission and the prosecutorial reform. Many PPP lawmakers are now going to Olympic Park to support Jang and his supporters. 
Also, there doesn’t seem to be a viable alternative to Jang in shepherding the PPP. Even if his critics successfully pressure Jang to step down and hold a national convention, he is most likely to win again. Votes from registered party members provide 70 percent of the chair vote tally, while performance in national polls is only worth 30 percent. Han may be more popular with the general public, but it’s Jang that holds a powerful grip on the PPP voters. 
Meanwhile, unlike throughout June and early July, anti-Han feelings are rearing up again. Han’s hero narrative is that he, as the PPP leader at the time of Yoon’s unconstitutional martial law, urged the PPP legislators to hightail it to the National Assembly and revoke Yoon’s martial law. The PPP lawmakers find this storytelling – where they were being wishy-washy, only to be jolted to sense and action by Han – not only irritating but also hurtful to the party’s unity. The issue boiled over again recently. 
Former PPP floor leader Choo Kyung-ho is currently on trial for allegedly aiding Yoon’s failed self-coup. On the night of Yoon’s declaration of martial law, on the PPP chat Choo messaged his fellow legislators to report to the party headquarters, rather than the National Assembly where they could vote against Yoon’s martial law. On July 9, Ahn Chul-soo, quite a popular PPP lawmaker, testified in favor of Choo that “I heard that Han ordered others to meet up at the party headquarters, and then Choo just followed along.”
In citing the PPP group chat and live media reports at the time, Han retorted that “just because some time has passed doesn’t mean that you can distort facts.” 
Ahn was livid. In a press conference, Ahn reminded Han that “he wasn’t the only one that night that blocked martial law.” Ahn chastised Han that it was unconscionable to attack fellow PPP personnel “just to protect his own epic.” Ahn is a four-time PPP legislator, with significant party clout and fans. Their spat engendered a fresh concern that Han’s rejoining the PPP will only foment discord. Ahn made it clear that “I’m categorically opposed to Han’s return to the PPP.”
Whether or not Han makes it back to the PPP, it seems most likely that Han and Jang would be incompatible. In early July, Jang’s young granddaughter passed away. Han dropped by the funeral, unannounced. Jang’s representatives expressed severe displeasure. Their political feud is now personal. 
But in Jang’s mind, the issue of Han is already a life-or-death matter. Regarding severing ties with Yoon and compromising with Han, he said that “doing these things means abandoning my identity and dying.”

A couple of days later, amid his supporters’ cheers and camera flicks, he lingered before the granite steps leading up to the National Assembly. Back in January, the PPP kicked Han out over allegations that the former party leader mobilized his family to slander former President Yoon Suk-yeol and his wife online. But in reality, it was more because Jang Dong-hyuk, the new PPP leader and a staunch Yoon supporter, didn’t want to see Han stirring up intra-party dissent over his leadership. 
Han led the PPP from December 2023 to April 2024 and then again from July to December 2024. During his leadership, Han locked horns with Yoon and openly defied Yoon’s martial law declaration and failed self-coup in December 2024.

articles.title: As the World Courts Beijing, Namibia Shows How Africa Can Sharpen Its China Strategy
articles.full_text:
A recent state visit offers lessons for African governments on how to translate high-level diplomacy into industrial partnerships, value addition, and development outcomes.
Chinese President Xi Jinping walks with Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah during a welcome ceremony at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China, July 10, 2026.
Since the start of 2026, few capitals have seen more diplomatic traffic than Beijing. A non-stop stream of world leaders has arrived seeking to deepen or recalibrate relations with China. Beyond the most headline-grabbing visits by U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, leaders from Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain, Uruguay, Ireland, South Korea, Vietnam, Serbia, and the United Arab Emirates, among others, have all made their way to China with distinct objectives in mind. 
This burst of diplomatic engagement has take place against a backdrop of mounting global uncertainty caused by trade disputes, geopolitical tensions, and supply chain disruptions. As one of the world’s largest trading nations, home to some of the most complete industrial and manufacturing ecosystems, and a key node in global supply chains, the appeal of China is clear.
Yet this global trend has received far less attention for its implications for Africa, even as African leaders and senior officials – including Mozambique’s President Daniel Chapo, Liberia’s Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti, Seychelles’ Foreign Minister Barry Faure, and South Africa’s Deputy President Paulus Mashatile – have also traveled to China this year.
African governments cannot assume that the diplomatic status quo will remain unchanged. The most recent visit by President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah from Namibia – a country of about 3.1 million people in the western corner of southern Africa – provides a useful lens through which to examine how African countries can strengthen their development objectives in this increasingly competitive diplomatic environment. 
Nandi-Ndaitwah made China one of her first major international destinations after taking office, helping to maintain momentum from previous administrations, strengthen relationships with Chinese counterparts, and reassure investors that long-term cooperation remains a priority.
More importantly, Nandi-Ndaitwah brought with her a clear agenda.
The first notable feature of her visit was the structure of the itinerary itself. The Namibian delegation began their week-long journey in Guangdong and Sichuan provinces before concluding in the capital. This approach was significant because the selected destinations were closely connected to China’s regional strengths and Namibia’s own development priorities. Guangdong, China’s leading province by economic output and a pioneer of the “reform and opening up” policy, provided exposure to one of the country’s most dynamic manufacturing, technology, and business ecosystems. 
In Sichuan, the delegation’s visit to local agricultural research facilities reflected Namibia’s interest in practical solutions to food security challenges, including drought-resistant crop varieties, agricultural technology, and modern farming equipment. The province has already been involved in advancing cooperation with Namibia in areas such as lithium resource development, biomass power projects, and green ammonia initiatives.
Second, local processing and value addition emerged as recurring themes throughout the visit. A notable example was Nandi-Ndaitwah’s delegation’s tour of the Daya Bay Nuclear Power Base in Shenzhen, which is managed by China General Nuclear Power Corporation, the operator of Namibia’s Husab Uranium Mine – one of China’s largest single industrial investments in Africa. 
Importantly, Namibia’s interest extends beyond attracting investment in resource extraction. The delegation used the visit to explore opportunities for greater domestic value addition, including seeking Chinese support to develop local uranium processing and enrichment capabilities. This reflects a broader shift in African countries’ expectations of China, from supplying it with raw materials to participating more deeply in global value chains through industrial upgrading and technology cooperation.
Namibia has positioned green hydrogen as a strategic pillar of its green industrialization agenda, seeking to leverage renewable energy resources for domestic value addition and industrial transformation. While Europe has become a key partner, progress in aligning European investment with Namibia’s broader industrialization ambitions has been slower than anticipated. To date, most large commercial initiatives have remained primarily export-oriented, with comparatively limited investment in downstream manufacturing and domestic value chains relative to Namibia’s stated objectives.
Hence, Namibia ensured this priority was elevated during Nandi-Ndaitwah’s meeting with President Xi Jinping n Beijing, and green hydrogen featured as a new strategic area for future bilateral cooperation. During the visit, Nandi-Ndaitwah also held discussions with representatives from China National Chemical Engineering Corporation in Sichuan, building upon existing cooperation with Namibia’s Hyphen Hydrogen Energy. The discussions further sought to accelerate the implementation of a 2025 signed Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) and an Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) contract for a green ammonia facility with an annual production capacity of 2.4 million tonnes. 
For context, it should be noted that the FEED and EPC contract are on par with the comprehensive cooperation agreement between Mozambique and China. In that relationship, Mozambique’s Rovuma Basin and its 5 trillion cubic meters of natural gas, along with significant deposits of critical minerals, drives cooperation in security, local processing capacity, and value chain boosting.
In these two special ways – ensuring a “beyond Beijing,” implementation-focused agenda and the intentionality behind the visit – Namibia demonstrated that it was not engaging with China from a position of weakness. The structure of the agreements, the sectors prioritized, and the language of mutual modernization and local value addition collectively indicate an awareness that Namibia’s leverage lies not only in attracting Chinese capital but in helping China achieve objectives it already has – whether securing critical mineral supply chains or advancing green technologies. Namibia increasingly frames the relationship as one of mutual strategic utility rather than one-way economic assistance.
The 2024 FOCAC Summit elevated China’s relations with all African countries maintaining diplomatic ties with Beijing to the level of “strategic relations,” providing an important institutional foundation for future cooperation. However, institutional ties alone do not guarantee outcomes. The challenge is how African governments can ensure that engagement translates into tangible development gains. 
One of the strongest messages African governments can bring to Beijing is that Africa is not merely seeking investment or aid; it can also help China advance its own strategic objectives. As China seeks to diversify its economic relationships and reduce overdependence on any single supplier, market, or region, Africa’s resource endowments, growing markets, and industrial potential create opportunities for deeper cooperation. Moreover, many African countries retain greater policy autonomy than regions where relations with China are increasingly shaped by geopolitical competition. This flexibility is a distinctive advantage, enabling African countries to pursue cooperation with China on terms aligned with their own development priorities. 
With preparations for the next phase of China–Africa cooperation already underway, with the Republic of the Congo in the helm as FOCAC co-chair for 2027, opportunities to shape future agenda are emerging. Countries that approach China with clear priorities, concrete projects, and sector-specific proposals will be better positioned to shape the direction of cooperation.

articles.title: Malaysia Orders UN Agency to Pause Registration of New Refugees
articles.full_text:
With the creation of a new refugee agency in January, the country has asserted its control over the processing of asylum-seekers.
Malaysia has asked the United Nations refugee ‌agency to temporarily stop registering new refugees in the country, as it begins running its own system for managing asylum-seekers, an official from the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday.
Deputy Foreign Minister Lukanisman Awang Sauni told parliament that the decision was made by the Cabinet so that the government could begin implementing ​its own refugee registration program.
Known as Dokumen Pendaftaran Pelarian (DPP), the program came into force in January, and is intended to replace the current registration system managed by the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
“We have gone through the Cabinet’s decision and instructed the UNHCR to stop any refugee registrations for the time being because we are reorganizing the implementation of the DPP program,” Lukanisman said, the Malaysian state news agency Bernama reported.
“Through the DPP, the government can manage data in a more organized manner, including the purposes of data coordination, identity verification, monitoring, and regulation without relying on the records of any foreign entities,” he added.
The UNHCR says that there were around 215,600 refugees and asylum-seekers registered with the agency in Malaysia, as of the end of February. The majority of these – some 193,824 – were from Myanmar, including 126,144 Rohingyas, 15,774 Chins, and 33,002 members of other ethnic groups who have fled persecution and conflict.
The introduction of the DPP follows several years in which Malaysia has significantly tightened the enforcement of its immigration laws, ramping up raids and arrests of those it deems to have entered the country illegally. This campaign peaked last year, when Malaysian authorities arrested about 92,000 undocumented migrants, compared with 12,000 in 2021.
Around 21,000 people are currently being held in immigration detention centers, with no legal limit on the length of their detention. The government has denied UNHCR access to these centers since 2019.
This has been paralleled in recent months by a growing public hostility toward Rohingya refugees in particular. As Alex Howlett reported for The Diplomat last week, last month more than half a million people signed a petition on Change.org calling for the removal of Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, while prominent public figures have recently described the Rohingya as “criminals” and “intruders” and likened them to a “cancer” on the country.
Lukanisman told parliament that the purpose of DPP was to reduce the burden on Malaysia of managing such a large number of asylum-seekers, and to exercise much tighter control over those who are admitted. Refugee registrations under the DPP “will be carried out through a strict process in collaboration with various enforcement agencies to ensure that only eligible individuals are registered and to prevent the entry of illegal immigrants in the future,” Bernama paraphrased him as saying.
Lukanisman said that the temporary halt to registrations would allow the UNHCR to focus on resettling already registered refugees in third countries, if they cannot be repatriated to their home nations, which is likely to be the case with the Rohingya and many of the other refugees from Myanmar. He added that authorities would continue regularly to engage and cooperate with UNHCR’s office in Malaysia.
Meanwhile, Lukanisman said that around 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently in the immigration detention depot are set to be repatriated as soon as Myanmar is ready to accept them.
“Approximately 5,000 Myanmar nationals who are currently detained at the depot will be repatriated to the Myanmar government and will be sent back using naval ships, subject to the resolution process,” he said.
On its website, UNHCR describes the new DPP program as “an important step towards a structured, predictable, and nationally owned approach to protecting people forced to flee their country.” It says that it is “committed to supporting its implementation through technical advice, capacity sharing and cooperation, drawing on international standards and comparative practices.”
However, the new program is a clear attempt by Malaysia’s government to take control of its immigration policy, out of a belief that UNHCR’s is applying too liberal criteria as to who can be granted refugee status. (Malaysia is not a signatory of the 1951 Refugee Convention.) It also reflects concerns about the growing difficulty of resettling refugees in third countries, particularly due to severe cuts to refugee admissions by the United States.
Unsurprisingly, human rights groups expressed concerns about the possible impact of both the DPP program, and yesterday’s order for UNHCR to cease refugee registrations, which they said created a lot of uncertainties for those seeking asylum in future.
Divya Shesshsan Balakrishnan, a spokesperson for Amnesty International Malaysia, said in a statement that Malaysia “should immediately clarify how asylum-seekers are to seek protection while UNHCR registration is suspended.” She also said that it should be transparent about “the assessment processes applied to those facing return to Myanmar, and ensure that no one is returned before their protection needs have been fully and fairly assessed.”
In February 2021, Malaysia deported 1,086 Myanmar nationals, ignoring a court order granting a temporary stay against their return. Rights groups said that this cohort included UNHCR-registered refugees.

articles.title: Nine Years in Limbo: Why Rohingya Repatriation Remains Stalled
articles.full_text:
An analysis of the political, legal, security, and geopolitical dimensions of the Rohingya crisis.
Newly arrived Rohingya refugees wait in line at a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, hoping to receive assistance from humanitarian aid groups, Feb. 25, 2025.
Nearly nine years after the 2017 military crackdown that forced more than 750,000 Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh, the prospect of their repatriation to Myanmar remains as distant as ever. Bangladesh recently took an important institutional step by establishing a national committee to strengthen coordination and develop a comprehensive strategy for the safe, voluntary, and sustainable return of the Rohingya. The initiative reflects Dhaka’s continued commitment to resolving one of the world’s most protracted refugee crises, after hosting more than 1.2 million Rohingya for nearly a decade.
The committee deserves recognition, but better coordination within Bangladesh alone cannot resolve a crisis the roots of which lie across the border. Rohingya repatriation is not primarily a logistical or humanitarian challenge. It is a political, legal, security, judicial, and geopolitical problem that demands structural change inside Myanmar and sustained international engagement. Until the conditions that drove the Rohingya from their homes are fundamentally addressed, large-scale return will remain unattainable.
The first and most essential requirement is the restoration of citizenship. Myanmar’s 1982 Citizenship Law effectively rendered the Rohingya stateless, stripping them of legal recognition and the rights associated with nationality. Citizenship is the foundation of freedom of movement, political participation, access to education and healthcare, property ownership, and equal protection under the law. Returning Rohingya refugees to Myanmar as stateless people, without restoring these rights, would simply recreate the conditions that enabled their persecution in the first place.
Security is equally indispensable. Since the 2021 military coup, Rakhine State has become a fragmented conflict zone divided between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army. This raises questions that no repatriation plan has adequately answered. Who will guarantee the safety of returning refugees? Who will issue citizenship documents and administer civilian institutions? Who will investigate human rights violations if they recur? Without credible and independently verifiable guarantees from either party, repatriation cannot be considered safe or sustainable.
Justice is another indispensable pillar of any durable solution. The atrocities committed against the Rohingya, including genocide, crimes against humanity, and decades of systematic discrimination, cannot simply be set aside in pursuit of political expediency. Accountability is not separate from repatriation; it is one of the conditions that makes repatriation possible. Without justice, trust cannot be rebuilt, and the structural drivers of persecution are likely to persist.
Equally important is the restoration of homes, land, and livelihoods. Thousands of Rohingya villages have been destroyed or occupied, leaving many refugees with nowhere to return. A meaningful return requires restitution or fair compensation, together with access to housing, education, healthcare, and sustainable livelihoods. Repatriation should enable refugees to rebuild dignified lives rather than merely cross an international border.
Finally, the Rohingya themselves must be at the center of any decision about their future. For too long, discussions have been dominated by governments and international organizations while the voices of refugees have remained marginal. Any repatriation process must be voluntary, informed, and based on genuine consent, free from coercion, political pressure, or declining humanitarian assistance.
Yet even if these conditions are widely recognized, they remain difficult to achieve because of the geopolitical realities surrounding Myanmar.
China remains Myanmar’s most influential international partner, and Rakhine State occupies an important position in the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor under the Belt and Road Initiative. Beijing has repeatedly facilitated dialogue between Bangladesh and Myanmar and promoted repatriation frameworks, but none has produced meaningful progress. China’s overriding priority is regional stability and the protection of strategic infrastructure, including the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and energy corridors connecting the Indian Ocean with Yunnan Province. Consequently, Beijing has shown little willingness to exert sustained pressure on Myanmar over citizenship, accountability, or ethnic rights, while its position at the United Nations Security Council has frequently shielded Myanmar from stronger international action.
India’s approach has been shaped by similar strategic calculations. Its Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project, which links Kolkata to Rakhine State’s Sittwe Port via India’s northeastern states, passes through territory increasingly controlled by the Arakan Army. As fighting has reshaped the political landscape in Rakhine, New Delhi has reportedly engaged with the Arakan Army to protect this vital connectivity project despite growing allegations of abuses against Rohingya civilians. Like China, India has prioritized regional stability, border security, and infrastructure over sustained pressure for structural reforms that would enable the Rohingya to return safely.
Although China and India compete for influence across Myanmar and Bangladesh, neither has consistently used its leverage to advance Rohingya rights. Instead, both have largely treated the crisis through the lens of strategic competition, economic connectivity, and regional security. This convergence has left Bangladesh with limited diplomatic leverage despite bearing the greatest part of the humanitarian burden.
Regional institutions have likewise struggled to respond effectively. ASEAN remains constrained by its long-standing principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of member states. Despite diplomatic initiatives and repeated statements, the organization has been unable to generate meaningful pressure capable of changing realities inside Myanmar.
By contrast, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) has pursued one of the most significant legal responses to the crisis. Acting with the support of the OIC, The Gambia filed proceedings against Myanmar before the International Court of Justice in 2019, alleging violations of the Genocide Convention. Meanwhile, the International Criminal Court continues to investigate alleged crimes involving the forced deportation of the Rohingya into Bangladesh. These legal processes represent important steps toward accountability, but they move slowly and have yet to produce changes that improve conditions for refugees contemplating return.
While diplomacy and litigation continue, conditions inside the refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar are steadily deteriorating. More than 1.2 million Rohingya remain dependent on humanitarian assistance, while renewed violence in Myanmar has driven additional refugees into Bangladesh since 2024. Repeated funding shortfalls have resulted in reduced food assistance, cuts to health services, and weakened protection programs. At the same time, camp violence, gender-based violence, trafficking, and criminal activity have become increasingly serious concerns. The absence of education, livelihoods, and long-term opportunities has driven some refugees to undertake dangerous sea journeys in search of safety and work elsewhere in the region.
The consequences extend beyond the camps themselves. Bangladesh’s host communities continue to face significant economic, environmental, and social pressures, while prolonged displacement increases the risk of regional instability and transnational security challenges. Humanitarian assistance remains indispensable, but it cannot resolve a crisis whose underlying causes remain unaddressed inside Myanmar.
Taken together, these realities explain why moves toward repatriation remain stalled. Myanmar has failed to restore citizenship, guarantee security, or ensure accountability. The fragmentation of authority in Rakhine has further complicated negotiations. China and India have prioritized strategic interests over structural reform. ASEAN has proved institutionally constrained. International justice mechanisms continue to move slowly, while donor fatigue has weakened humanitarian support. Each of these factors reinforces the others, creating a cycle in which the crisis is managed rather than resolved.
Bangladesh’s new repatriation committee represents an important institutional initiative and demonstrates the country’s continued commitment to pursuing a durable solution. However, even the most effective national coordination cannot substitute for political transformation inside Myanmar.
The success of repatriation ultimately depends on whether those returning can do so with equal rights, legal protection, personal security, and the opportunity to rebuild their lives in dignity. Until those conditions are met, repatriation will remain more a diplomatic aspiration than a practical reality, leaving more than 1 million Rohingya trapped in prolonged limbo.
Nearly nine years after the 2017 military crackdown that forced more than 750,000 Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh, the prospect of their repatriation to Myanmar remains as distant as ever. Bangladesh recently took an important institutional step by establishing a national committee to strengthen coordination and develop a comprehensive strategy for the safe, voluntary, and sustainable return of the Rohingya. The initiative reflects Dhaka’s continued commitment to resolving one of the world’s most protracted refugee crises, after hosting more than 1.2 million Rohingya for nearly a decade.
The committee deserves recognition, but better coordination within Bangladesh alone cannot resolve a crisis the roots of which lie across the border. Rohingya repatriation is not primarily a logistical or humanitarian challenge. It is a political, legal, security, judicial, and geopolitical problem that demands structural change inside Myanmar and sustained international engagement. Until the conditions that drove the Rohingya from their homes are fundamentally addressed, large-scale return will remain unattainable.
The first and most essential requirement is the restoration of citizenship. Myanmar’s 1982 Citizenship Law effectively rendered the Rohingya stateless, stripping them of legal recognition and the rights associated with nationality. Citizenship is the foundation of freedom of movement, political participation, access to education and healthcare, property ownership, and equal protection under the law. Returning Rohingya refugees to Myanmar as stateless people, without restoring these rights, would simply recreate the conditions that enabled their persecution in the first place.
Security is equally indispensable. Since the 2021 military coup, Rakhine State has become a fragmented conflict zone divided between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army. This raises questions that no repatriation plan has adequately answered. Who will guarantee the safety of returning refugees? Who will issue citizenship documents and administer civilian institutions? Who will investigate human rights violations if they recur? Without credible and independently verifiable guarantees from either party, repatriation cannot be considered safe or sustainable.
Justice is another indispensable pillar of any durable solution. The atrocities committed against the Rohingya, including genocide, crimes against humanity, and decades of systematic discrimination, cannot simply be set aside in pursuit of political expediency. Accountability is not separate from repatriation; it is one of the conditions that makes repatriation possible. Without justice, trust cannot be rebuilt, and the structural drivers of persecution are likely to persist.
Equally important is the restoration of homes, land, and livelihoods. Thousands of Rohingya villages have been destroyed or occupied, leaving many refugees with nowhere to return. A meaningful return requires restitution or fair compensation, together with access to housing, education, healthcare, and sustainable livelihoods. Repatriation should enable refugees to rebuild dignified lives rather than merely cross an international border.
Finally, the Rohingya themselves must be at the center of any decision about their future. For too long, discussions have been dominated by governments and international organizations while the voices of refugees have remained marginal. Any repatriation process must be voluntary, informed, and based on genuine consent, free from coercion, political pressure, or declining humanitarian assistance.
Yet even if these conditions are widely recognized, they remain difficult to achieve because of the geopolitical realities surrounding Myanmar.

articles.title: Rhyu Si-min, Once Lee Jae-myung’s Champion, Turns on the President He Helped Elect
articles.full_text:
The liberal commentator’s escalating attacks on President Lee have opened a rare split inside South Korea’s ruling Democratic Party.
Rhyu Si-min, a former minister of health and welfare, has spent the past few decades building a reputation as one of South Korea’s most influential liberal commentators. Over the past several weeks, however, he shockingly has aimed that influence at President Lee Jae-myung – the leader his commentary once helped elect.
In a series of YouTube appearances since late June, Rhyu has argued that Lee is not merely tolerating the ruling Democratic Party’s drift toward the center but directing it. He compared the shift to the “reconstruction” of a building that displaced longtime residents without their consent and predicted that Lee would come out damaged and the party would descend into disarray. 
Rhyu pressed further on July 21, saying that the informal bloc of Lee loyalists known as “New Lee Jae-myung” answers not to junior lawmakers but to the president himself. He argued that the disorder inside the party over the past year most likely traces back to a plan Lee set in motion from his first days in office. Rhyu also compared the presidential Blue House to a fish market that would start to smell of rot without outside scrutiny. 
While accusing Lee of betraying his loyal supporters in the DP, Rhyu’s most detailed accusation concerns prosecutorial reform. He has argued that a stalled bill to fully separate police investigative power from prosecutorial indictment power remains unfinished because Lee himself wants prosecutors to keep some investigative authority, and that Lee has let allies absorb the criticism rather than explain the shift in his own voice. The presidential Blue House pushed back immediately, saying its commitment to full separation of investigation and indictment powers has never wavered.
The remarks have unsettled South Korea’s ruling party, which is already bracing for a leadership election on August 17. A group of pro-Lee lawmakers dismissed Rhyu as a false prophet. Two of the three contenders for the DP chair election – Kim Min-seok, Song Young-gil, and Jung Cheong-rae – have weighed in as well. Kim, a former prime minister for Lee and fourth-time lawmaker, pushed back by saying that Rhyu’s account of the president’s motives was not accurate. Song, a veteran lawmaker and former mayor of Incheon, also said Rhyu’s language crossed into curses and invective. However, Jung, the former leader of the DP, did not make any comments on Rhyu’s controversial remarks, showing his stance on this recent series of events. 
To no one’s surprise, Rhyu has not backed down.
Rhyu, 66, first entered politics as a student activist at Seoul National University in the 1980s as part of the democratic movements against the military dictatorship. He later served two terms in the National Assembly and led the Ministry of Health and Welfare under President Roh Moo-hyun from 2006 to 2007. 
After losing a series of races in the years that followed, he declared his retirement from electoral politics in 2013 and returned to writing, his first job. He is currently one of the best-selling authors in the country. Rhyu has also built a large following as a television debate panelist and one of the country’s most-watched YouTube commentators. He went on to chair the Roh Moo-hyun Foundation, a role that cemented his standing as a leading voice on Roh in the liberal bloc.
Using his role as a liberal thought leader, Rhyu was an active figure in the rise of Lee Jae-myung. Rhyu was a fixture on debate programs and YouTube broadcasts that helped consolidate liberal support behind Lee’s candidacy – and Rhyu has said so himself. 
Why he has now turned that platform against the man he helped install? His own remarks – and the reactions they have provoked inside the liberal bloc – provide clues.
Rhyu has repeatedly framed his criticism as an insider’s disappointment rather than an outsider’s attack. He has said he still considers himself a Lee supporter and wants the president to succeed even as he insists Lee’s course will fail. That framing reflects a belief that his own advocacy carried real weight in Lee’s election and that he therefore has standing to correct a course he sees as reckless. When Lee’s approval ratings fell faster than the DP’s own, Rhyu pointed to that gap as evidence the president, not the party, bears responsibility.
Also, Rhyu has cast the conflict as a struggle between the party’s traditional base, rooted in the democracy movement of the 1980s and the Roh Moo-hyun–Moon Jae-in political lineage, and a newer bloc of centrist supporters who joined behind Lee. He argued that this newer group has spent months attacking the party’s core cells online, likening the discord as a kind of autoimmune disease. Rhyu pointed to personnel decisions as evidence of the rightward drift, arguing that officials who mock or distance themselves from former South Korean President Moon have been rewarded, starting with Lee’s pick to lead the personnel authority of the government. According to Rhyu, conservative figures have been brought into government in ways that leave it unclear whether the outreach is genuine or aimed at remaking the identity of the DP.
As a longtime figure in the Roh-Moon camp, Rhyu appears uneasy watching that lineage lose influence inside a party now led by Lee loyalists. It’s a bit ironic, then, that Rhyu is reportedly not a member of the DP, but an independent. 
With that in mind, Rhyu’s commentary about Cho Kuk, the former justice minister for Moon and founder of the Rebuilding Korea Party, is noteworthy. Cho finished third in a June 3 by-election in Pyeongtaek, a race widely seen as winnable for the broader liberal bloc. Instead, the conservative candidate won, as the DP and Rebuilding Korea Party split the liberal vote. Cho stepped down as leader of his party over the loss. The defeat came after Jung failed to garner support within his party for a merger with Cho’s party. 
Rhyu has treated that sequence as a warning sign for the DP’s future rather than a verdict on Cho’s own campaign. His sympathy for Cho, whom he has grouped with Moon, Jung and broadcaster Kim Ou-joon as targets of the same online attacks, suggests he sees rebuilding a path back to power for Cho as part of what is at stake in the current infighting. 
Meanwhile, Rhyu’s most pointed remarks have landed just as the party’s leadership race has begun. Several of Rhyu’s own critics inside the party have suggested, without offering proof, that his commentary is meant to boost Jung’s standing at the expense of Lee-aligned rivals like Kim and Song. Rhyu has not confirmed that motive and he has said that he does not expect to win the argument so much as to put an uncomfortable truth on the record. Still, the proximity of his broadsides to the chair election has done little to quiet suspicion.
Whether any of these explanations is sufficient on its own is unclear. Rhyu himself has offered a simpler account: he believes Lee’s strategy will fail and he says so because no one else with his standing will. The DP’s leadership vote on August 17 is now about more than electing its next chair; the outcome will help demonstrate how much weight Rhyu’s warnings still carry with the base he helped build. If Jung becomes the next leader of the DP, it will be a clear message that even the president himself is not the core of the party – it’s those in the Roh-Moon lineage.

articles.title: Ladakh Cannot Afford a Plastic Future
articles.full_text:
A broken system continues to push disposable plastic into one of the world’s most fragile mountain ecosystems.
Students collects trash during The Himalayan Cleanup campaign, ahead of World Environment Day, in Gangtok, India, May 29, 2023.
Every cleanup in Ladakh, India, tells the same story. Volunteers arrive expecting pristine mountains, crystal-clear streams, and breathtaking landscapes, only to find colorful snack wrappers buried in the soil, plastic bottles washed into rivers, and food packaging scattered across mountain slopes. Visitors move on, but leave their rubbish behind.
More than just a litter problem, this is evidence of a broken system that continues to push disposable plastic into one of the world’s most fragile mountain ecosystems while expecting local communities to manage the consequences. 
The evidence gathered through The Himalayan Cleanup (THC) 2025 and 2026, coordinated by Little Green World, Navikru Eco Foundation, and local stakeholders, leaves little room for doubt. In 2025, volunteers cleaned 59 sites across Ladakh and documented 22,582 waste items, with more than 21,000 of which were plastic. Just over 74 percent of the plastic collected was non-recyclable. 
One year later, THC 2026 painted an equally worrying picture. Across 19 cleanup sites, 1,050 volunteers from 23 schools and organizations collected 19,521 waste items, of which 18,709 (95.8 percent) were plastic. Even more alarming, 75.6 percent of this plastic was non-recyclable, while 71.5 percent consisted of multilayer packaging – the wrappers used for chips, biscuits, confectionery and other everyday products that have little recycling value. 
Importantly, food packaging accounted for 73 percent of all plastic collected, followed by smoking-related products (18.7 percent) and personal care products (7.1 percent). These are products consumed within minutes, whose packaging can remain in the environment for decades.
In Ladakh’s cold-desert ecosystem, where decomposition is slow and waste infrastructure is limited, plastic accumulates in the landscape, contaminates water sources, threatens wildlife, and often ends up being openly burned, releasing toxic pollutants into the air. 
Perhaps the most important finding from the cleanup is where most of the plastic came from. Brand audits repeatedly identified packaging from major companies, including ITC, PepsiCo, Nestlé, Coca-Cola, Perfetti Van Melle, Parle Agro, Britannia, Haldiram’s, GCMMF (Amul), Mondelez, and Dabur India. 
This is not about blaming individual companies. It is about recognizing that corporations benefiting from the sale of packaged products in Ladakh must also share responsibility for recovering and managing the waste those products generate. For too long, the responsibility has fallen almost entirely on schools, volunteers, local communities, and municipal workers. Every year they organize cleanup drives, collect thousands of pieces of plastic, and restore the landscape – only to repeat the same effort the following year. 
Cleanup campaigns are essential because they build awareness and generate evidence, but they cannot solve a problem rooted in unsustainable production and consumption. Ladakh does not need more cleanups alone; it needs stronger policies and shared responsibility. 
The Ladakh Administration and policymakers must strengthen Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) by ensuring that companies finance the collection and recycling of the packaging they introduce into the region, while prioritizing absolute caps on plastic production. Producers of such disposable consumer goods cannot recycle their way out of this crisis; they must actively phase out single-use packaging altogether and invest heavily in toxic-free, reusable delivery systems, instead of shifting the burden onto mountain communities. 
The tourism sector – including hotels, restaurants, and tour operators – must also reduce its dependence on single-use plastics by promoting refill stations and reusable alternatives. Consumers also have a role to play by choosing reusable products, segregating waste, and demanding sustainable packaging from the brands they support. 
Ladakh did not create this plastic problem, and it should not be expected to solve it alone.

articles.title: The G7’s Indo-Pacific Gap and Trump’s 2027 Opportunity
articles.full_text:
Two of the countries best positioned to contribute to the G7’s expanded agenda remain outside the group’s permanent membership.
The G7 has changed almost everything – except its membership. Created in the 1970s to coordinate among the largest industrial democracies, its agenda has become impressively expansive. Canada’s G7 presidency in 2025 produced initiatives on critical minerals and artificial intelligence. France’s 2026 presidency has placed economic security, supply chain resilience, global imbalances, development partnerships, and new technology risks at the center of the group’s work. 
The G7’s agenda has moved into the 21st century. Its composition still reflects the late 20th.
The G7 has tried to compensate through guest invitations and issue-specific outreach. That flexibility is valuable, but it does not provide continuity, agenda-setting authority, or responsibility for implementation. A country invited to one summit may disappear from next year’s. Guest invitations can widen participation, but this cannot correct a persistent membership mismatch.
And two of the countries best positioned to contribute to the G7’s expanded agenda, South Korea and Australia, remain outside the group’s permanent membership.
South Korea is the world’s 13th-largest economy and a pivotal producer in semiconductors, batteries, shipbuilding, nuclear energy, digital infrastructure, and defense manufacturing. When the G7 discusses chip supply, maritime industrial capacity, advanced manufacturing, or North Korea, South Korea’s participation is indispensable.
Australia brings a different but equally important set of assets: critical minerals, energy, maritime geography, development partnerships in the Pacific, AUKUS, and a growing network of economic-security and defense agreements across the Indo-Pacific. A G7 strategy for trusted mineral supply chains that excludes Australia is incomplete from the start. 
An original dataset I compiled using more than 300 publicly available indicators covering economic scale, technological capacity, defense contribution, governance, development finance, supply chain relevance, and democratic performance shows that South Korea and Australia meet or exceed several existing G7 members across many of the issues where the group now claims to lead.
This creates an unusual opportunity in 2027, when the United States assumes the G7 presidency. The Trump administration is an unlikely champion of multilateral reform in the traditional sense. But the relevant question is whether enlargement can be presented as a better deal for the United States.
The answer is yes. South Korea and Australia are U.S. treaty allies that already carry substantial burdens. They bring industrial capabilities, strategic geography, investment, and defense cooperation that Washington wants. Expansion can be framed not as widening a diplomatic club for its own sake, but as aligning membership with contribution. The Trump administration’s own fiscal year 2027 budget planning already recognizes U.S. hosting responsibilities. That creates a concrete deadline and a presidential platform.
During the U.S. presidency, the G7 should admit South Korea and Australia as full members. The G7’s legitimacy will not be restored by adding every important democracy, nor should enlargement become open-ended. The initial standard should be demanding: sustained democratic governance, advanced economic and technological capacity, willingness to provide international public goods, and direct relevance to the institution’s core agenda. South Korea and Australia satisfy all four.
The new “Democratic G9” should then create a light troika secretariat linking the previous, current, and next presidencies. The G7’s informality is useful, but annual rotation too often produces discontinuity. A small standing mechanism could preserve priorities, track implementation, and support working groups without turning the G9 into a treaty organization. Critical minerals projects, sanctions coordination, AI standards, and development-finance commitments all require follow-through beyond a single summit cycle.
The G9 should also institutionalize outreach to the Global South. Inviting a changing list of guests to one summit does not constitute representation. The G9 should establish recurring, issue-specific consultations with countries from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, and with China. On debt, food security, digital infrastructure, climate finance, and mineral development, partners should help shape agendas before leaders announce them. Enlargement of the democratic core must be paired with a more serious practice of consultation beyond it.
The first is that Trump will not support G7 enlargement. But a proposal built around burden sharing, China competition, supply chain resilience, and allied industrial capacity is more compatible with his politics than a defense of inherited membership. A U.S.-led expansion of the G7 could be framed not as an extension of liberalism, but as an American-led modernization of the institution.
The second is that the rise of BRICS makes the G7 irrelevant. The opposite is true. BRICS expansion demonstrates a demand for institutions that reflect a wider distribution of power.
The third is arbitrariness: why admit South Korea and Australia, but not India, Brazil, or others? The answer is that India and Brazil are indispensable global actors and should be central to structured outreach, but full membership in a democratic steering group requires a combination of regime standards, policy alignment, contribution, and institutional readiness. In our dataset, moreover, India, Brazil, and Indonesia do not yet perform at the level of G7 countries on the key issue-areas identified as critical by the group’s leaders. 
The G7’s problem is that it excludes countries that already perform essential functions while claiming authority over issues they help govern. The 2027 U.S. presidency offers a chance to correct that mismatch. 
A Democratic G9 would be a test of whether the advanced democracies can still adapt and rebuild global rules and norms before crisis makes such adaptation unavoidable.
This essay is one of four to emerge from discussions at an international conference jointly organized by the Seoul Forum for International Affairs and the Hairan Series of Korea University’s Institute for Interdisciplinary Unification Studies, “Democratic Multilateralism at the Edge,” held in Seoul on April 20, 2026. 
The G7 has changed almost everything – except its membership. Created in the 1970s to coordinate among the largest industrial democracies, its agenda has become impressively expansive. Canada’s G7 presidency in 2025 produced initiatives on critical minerals and artificial intelligence. France’s 2026 presidency has placed economic security, supply chain resilience, global imbalances, development partnerships, and new technology risks at the center of the group’s work. 
The G7’s agenda has moved into the 21st century. Its composition still reflects the late 20th.
The G7 has tried to compensate through guest invitations and issue-specific outreach. That flexibility is valuable, but it does not provide continuity, agenda-setting authority, or responsibility for implementation. A country invited to one summit may disappear from next year’s. Guest invitations can widen participation, but this cannot correct a persistent membership mismatch.
And two of the countries best positioned to contribute to the G7’s expanded agenda, South Korea and Australia, remain outside the group’s permanent membership.
South Korea is the world’s 13th-largest economy and a pivotal producer in semiconductors, batteries, shipbuilding, nuclear energy, digital infrastructure, and defense manufacturing. When the G7 discusses chip supply, maritime industrial capacity, advanced manufacturing, or North Korea, South Korea’s participation is indispensable.
Australia brings a different but equally important set of assets: critical minerals, energy, maritime geography, development partnerships in the Pacific, AUKUS, and a growing network of economic-security and defense agreements across the Indo-Pacific. A G7 strategy for trusted mineral supply chains that excludes Australia is incomplete from the start. 
An original dataset I compiled using more than 300 publicly available indicators covering economic scale, technological capacity, defense contribution, governance, development finance, supply chain relevance, and democratic performance shows that South Korea and Australia meet or exceed several existing G7 members across many of the issues where the group now claims to lead.
This creates an unusual opportunity in 2027, when the United States assumes the G7 presidency. The Trump administration is an unlikely champion of multilateral reform in the traditional sense. But the relevant question is whether enlargement can be presented as a better deal for the United States.
The answer is yes. South Korea and Australia are U.S. treaty allies that already carry substantial burdens. They bring industrial capabilities, strategic geography, investment, and defense cooperation that Washington wants. Expansion can be framed not as widening a diplomatic club for its own sake, but as aligning membership with contribution. The Trump administration’s own fiscal year 2027 budget planning already recognizes U.S. hosting responsibilities. That creates a concrete deadline and a presidential platform.
During the U.S. presidency, the G7 should admit South Korea and Australia as full members. The G7’s legitimacy will not be restored by adding every important democracy, nor should enlargement become open-ended. The initial standard should be demanding: sustained democratic governance, advanced economic and technological capacity, willingness to provide international public goods, and direct relevance to the institution’s core agenda. South Korea and Australia satisfy all four.
The new “Democratic G9” should then create a light troika secretariat linking the previous, current, and next presidencies. The G7’s informality is useful, but annual rotation too often produces discontinuity. A small standing mechanism could preserve priorities, track implementation, and support working groups without turning the G9 into a treaty organization. Critical minerals projects, sanctions coordination, AI standards, and development-finance commitments all require follow-through beyond a single summit cycle.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s National Security Law Comes for the Bookstores
articles.full_text:
The reorientation – and restriction – of the city’s once-vibrant civil society continues.
On July 15, the Hong Kong national security police raided two bookstores in Mong Kok: Have a Nice Stay (founded by former journalists) and Greenfield Bookstore. The police arrested five people on suspicion of selling seditious publications. 
This falls into a larger pattern of national security operations against bookstores, with Book Punch and Hunter Bookstore being targeted in March and June, respectively. Book Punch and Hunter are well-known and established bookstores within Hong Kong, and the government cracking down on them sends a signal to all independently operated bookstores and civic spaces. 
These raids represent a qualitative shift in the approach of the national security police, which had hitherto tolerated the existence of independent bookstores. The businesses in question were more than just bookstores; they functioned as semi-civic spaces, hosting typical events such as discussions and book talks but also yoga classes. Their function was to build and sustain a community, which became more difficult in Hong Kong amid the rapid breakdown of civil society following the 2020 National Security Law and the subsequent installation of a national security complex. The July 15 arrests were made under the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, which broadly outlined internal and external threats.
Independent bookstores in Hong Kong have a long history of being political. Hong Kong stores and publishers often served as a gateway to sell sensitive books that were censored in the mainland. Memoirs of political figures, for example, could be bought in street stalls easily visible to tourists from Mainland China. 
Not all independent bookstores have a political function, of course, but especially those founded in the wake of 2019 protests had a particular identity in mind. Many of them purposefully sought to foster an alternative civil society that became increasingly difficult to maintain. As I found in my research, they navigated Hong Kong’s national security clampdown starting in 2020 through delicate balancing acts such as the careful curation of books, community building, and calculated ambiguity. 
The recent prosecutions, however, show that the boundary of acceptable behavior has shifted once again. The book store Have a Nice Stay had already announced its closure before the raid took place, citing “uncertain red lines.” When it becomes arguably impossible to adapt, a decade-old model of cultural resistance begins to fade away, with consequences for what remains of Hong Kong civil society. 
For the authorities, there are benefits to maintaining what one could term strategic ambiguity. However, one might argue that even the national security police themselves do not know what or where the “red lines” are. Communities, civic spaces, and speech in Hong Kong will come under increasing examination as the government uses and ever-finer comb to find supposed threats. With the obvious targets out of the way, the range of what will be allowed seems set to shrink still further. Meanwhile, the police, whose budget has ballooned in the past years, need to justify their existence even as there is less and less to scrutinize.
The attention being paid to bookstores therefore shows a new development in the approach of the national security police toward perceived threats. Traditional loci of activism such as labor and student unions have already been dealt with in recent years, and now the gaze has shifted to spaces that are able to foster a sense of Hong Kong identity and society different from the one mandated by the government. 
Independent bookstores are particularly suspect because of the wares that they sell. Books hold powerful ideas, including alternatives to the status quo, which authoritarian governments are wary of. As Hong Kong society draws closer to that of Mainland China, it must also align with the idea that society’s direction and future is solely in the hands of the government. Hong Kong’s independent bookstores, especially those that explicitly identified themselves with the pro-democratic ethos of the 2019 protest movement, are remnants of an old Hong Kong society where discussion about the direction of society was still possible in public. 
These arrests must therefore be read as part of the larger integration of Hong Kong within the People’s Republic of China. Hong Kong was handed over to Beijing’s control in 1997, but full integration is scheduled to occur only by 2047, 50 years later. As Beijing prepares for that long-term goal, Hong Kong society and culture are currently being reconstructed. 
This includes major projects such as the “patriots governing Hong Kong” election reforms as well as the patriotic education reforms. But it also includes more banal examples, such as mandating that the Chinese national anthem must be played before news broadcasts, or the fact that October 1, China’s national day, has been a public holiday since 1997. Other, more visible changes include the complete renovation of the Hong Kong Museum of History to include a national security component.

While economic concerns previously served as a brake on such reforms, the 2019 protests and subsequent reaction have shown that ideology and stability by whatever means take precedence over economic development and global alignment. 
Hong Kong has come a long way from being the “goose that lays the golden eggs” that the Chinese Communist Party was careful not to touch. articles.title: Nepali PM Balendra Shah’s Image as a Change Agent is at Risk
articles.full_text:
Shah has shown less concern for the health and wellbeing of the poor, and is preoccupied with appearing as a ruthless executor of public plans.
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah (center) heads a meeting of the Council of Ministers in Kathmandu, Nepal, July 14, 2026.
When 37-year-old Prem Prasad Acharya died after setting himself on fire in January 2023, Balendra Shah was the mayor of Kathmandu, Nepal’s bustling national capital. Acharya had been frustrated by the repeated failures of his business ventures. At the time, Shah termed the incident a sign of “the state’s extreme failure.”
That comment is now coming back to haunt Shah, the country’s prime minister since March 2026.
On July 9 this year, it was the turn of 25-year-old Ganesh Nepali, a Dalit who was providing for his family by running a ride-hailing service on his motorcycle, to try to self-immolate. He chose to do so rather than pay 1,000 Nepali rupees (roughly $6.5) in parking fines. He died a day later. Nepali was seemingly under great financial stress as he had to support his family on his meager income while paying the bank installments on the bike. At the time of the incident, Nepali had been applying to work in the UAE.
Nearly two weeks later, Shah continues to feel the fallout from the incident.
The parking fine imposed by Kathmandu’s municipal police acted as the immediate trigger for Nepali, who was already under considerable financial strain.
During his term as mayor, Shah had given the municipal police dubious powers that are otherwise given only to traffic police, including the power to impose traffic fines — and those powers continue to be abused. Although the municipal police falls under the Kathmandu Metropolitan City and not under the federal government that Shah leads, its actions continue to be seen as part of Shah’s legacy as mayor.
The Ganesh Nepali controversy was especially damaging because the government at the time was defending proposals for a significant increase in the scope and amount of traffic violation fines, with top fines of 100,000 rupees for some offenses. Even before Nepali’s self-immolation, these proposed fines were widely being criticized as instruments of coercion rather than proportionate regulation.
Then there is the broader picture. Shah, who is now 36, came to power on the back of the youth protests partly fueled by concerns over unemployment and inequality. There has been no visible progress in addressing these problems. Young people remain frustrated by the lack of good jobs and are looking to leave the country the first chance they get.
There is no hard proof that the plight of those who are indebted or in precarious employment has gotten worse under the new government. Yet the youth frustration does expose the absence of a convincing government response to the old problems of indebtedness and joblessness.
Separately, soon after becoming prime minister, Shah started a campaign to raze Kathmandu’s riverside squatter settlements without any plan to resettle thousands of those who would be displaced. During the campaign, two squatters died by suicide.
Even during his tenure as the mayor of Kathmandu, the benefits of Shah’s efforts were most visible to the upper and middle classes, while their costs disproportionately fell on squatters and informal workers. The squatters were portrayed as usurpers of public land and bulldozers were turned on their homes. Other roadside vendors were also forcibly removed. His beautification and public-space campaigns were not matched by credible plans to protect housing and livelihoods.
As the prime minister, Shah has shown even less concern for the health and wellbeing of the poor. Rather, he seems determined to project an image of a ruthless executor of public plans. Critics of his government’s unjust plans and policies are often harassed by pro-Shah accounts online.
Another emblematic recent case of state excess has been the beating and detention of Majid Ansari, a young activist who had dared to speak up on the wretched plight of the displaced squatters. Ansari vociferously criticized the government when the temporary shelters where the squatters had been housed started flooding; the government had earlier moved them there despite warnings that the place was flood-prone.
Ansari was taken into custody on dubious charges — much to the anger of the Gen Z activists who had propelled Shah to power. Ansari was among the activists involved in the Gen Z movement that overthrew the old K.P. Sharma Oli government, an event that culminated in Shah’s election as prime minister in the March 2026 elections.
The Gen Z activists are not alone in criticizing the Shah government’s rather arbitrary and inhumane governance. Increasingly, even ruling-party lawmakers have been put off by the prime minister’s heavy-handedness and lack of foresight.
The government has yet to show that unemployment and inequality are among its urgent priorities; Nepali’s death crystallized the wider public frustrations.
Shah’s public image as a change agent is at risk. The prime minister always appears in public wearing his signature dark glasses. The glasses that once symbolized anti-establishment defiance have increasingly become a metaphor for a government unwilling to see those bearing the heaviest costs of its rule.

articles.title: New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar Is Not Tahrir Square, But It Can Become One
articles.full_text:
At its heart, this movement is demanding accountability, not upheaval.
Protestors gather at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, India, July 21, 2026.
It is tempting to compare the students’ protest at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar with Cairo’s Tahrir Square, the epicenter of the uprising that brought to an end Hosni Mubarak’s nearly 30-year rule.
The comparison, however, is only partly valid. Equating what is happening in New Delhi with Egypt’s iconic protest would be unrealistic, even if the two movements share striking similarities. In Egypt, calls to gather at Tahrir Square spread rapidly through social media, including YouTube and Facebook. Likewise, the Cockroach Janta Party, which emerged on Instagram, has used social media to mobilize thousands to assemble at Jantar Mantar and protest against the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) examination paper leak, which has fueled widespread anger among students and, according to the movement, contributed to a tragic wave of student suicides.
The objectives of the two protests, however, are fundamentally different. The protesters at Jantar Mantar are demanding accountability from the government and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The demonstrators in Tahrir Square sought nothing less than the end of Hosni Mubarak’s three-decade authoritarian rule. Yet the deeper similarity lies elsewhere: both movements are driven by the frustration of a generation that believes its government has become unresponsive to its aspirations and grievances.
The Jantar Mantar protest is not an attempt to overthrow the state, but a determined demand that the state honor its constitutional obligations and restore young people’s faith in public institutions. It is a physical mirror of a generation’s quiet desperation, where broken promises, shrinking opportunities, and unresponsive governance are finding a collective voice.
If the Egyptians were expressing their anger against Hosni Mubarak’s three-decade rule, during which every voice of dissent was often silenced by the butt of a gun, Jantar Mantar has lifted the lid on years of frustration over misgovernance and, perhaps more importantly, what many perceive as the arrogance of the Narendra Modi government over the past 14 years.
Calls for public accountability have frequently been met with disdain. Those seeking answers on corruption, administrative failures, or misgovernance are often dismissed, insulted, or humiliated rather than engaged with. The government’s response to successive examination paper leaks has done little to restore public confidence. Beyond transferring the education secretary to another department, no major structural reforms have been announced. Nor did Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan publicly reach out to assuage the feelings of the students who were forced to retake the examination after the paper leak.
Another feature that demonstrates public anger against the government is that people across India and abroad are using online food delivery apps such as Zomato and Swiggy to send bulk meals — ranging from pizzas and burgers to local snacks — directly to protesters at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi. This spontaneous act of solidarity has overwhelmed the protest site with food, prompting organizers to appeal to people to stop sending more. Perhaps the biggest sign of the movement’s growing public support is that people who are unable to join the protest physically are choosing to express their empathy and solidarity by sending food to the protesters.
The movement is gathering momentum with each passing day. As the authorities attempt to curb it through brute force, the protests have only grown stronger. The more the police and paramilitary forces resort to violence, the more determined and steadfast the protesters become. History offers many examples of governments inadvertently strengthening protest movements when they respond to public anger with force rather than dialogue. Democracies possess an advantage unavailable to authoritarian regimes — they can absorb dissent through accountability and reform. Whether this government chooses that path may determine whether Jantar Mantar remains a protest site or evolves into something far more politically significant.
Jantar Mantar today stands as a barometer of India’s social contract. When thousands of educated young people travel hundreds of miles to sleep on Delhi’s pavement, they are sending a clear message that the institutions meant to hear their voices — through petitions, representations, and democratic processes — have failed them.
At its heart, this movement is demanding accountability, not upheaval. It is asking the government to restore the promise that education, merit, and hard work will once again open the door to opportunity. Whether the Cockroach Janata Party survives as an organization is almost beside the point. The larger question is whether the government chooses to listen to the generation or not.
The roar of slogans at Jantar Mantar is growing louder. It is now for the government to break its silence before it’s too late.
