The lack of unanimity on key goals such as “joint[ly] combating terrorism” and “jointly searching for solutions to the problems that would arise in the 21st century” makes the SCO long on rhetoric but short on delivery. 
In particular, the India-Pakistan differences repeatedly cast a long shadow on the SCO’s workings, as do China-India disagreements concerning the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). During the defense ministers’ meeting in Bishkek, India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh spoke about “fractured world views” of “inward-looking countries,”  but also about how India “demonstrated its firm resolve that terrorism epicenters are no longer immune to justifiable punishment” – indirectly hinting at Pakistan. 
On July 17, India participated in the 12th Meeting of the Heads of Border Services of SCO member states, hosted in Islamabad under Pakistan’s chairmanship. The meeting was meant to exchange assessments on border security and finalize plans for the SCO’s joint border operation, “Solidarity 2026.” New Delhi’s long-standing apprehension that the SCO remains a forum for China-Pakistan nexus vis-à-vis India is bound to grow once the baton of SCO leadership passes over to Islamabad for the next year.   
Further, the wars in Ukraine and Iran have obligated the SCO to take a position on conflicts that have affected the economies of the world. This is in sync with the SCO’s identified goal of “cooperating in the prevention of international conflicts and their peaceful settlement.” However, having parties to these conflicts like Russia and Iran as members hasn’t led to much progress. 
It could be argued that such a state is hardly unique to SCO. Similar challenges afflict other such large groupings where members fail to balance collective goals against individual national interests. Multilateralism around the world has come under increasing strain and is mostly faltering.
articles.summary: In an era of diminishing multilateralism, can the SCO actually bring results?

articles.title: Why a Tibetan Protester Set Himself on Fire Outside the United Nations
articles.full_text:
Loga Rangzen’s self-immolation was intended to force Tibet back onto the international agenda. Instead, it exposed the challenges Tibetans face amid China’s growing global influence.
Members of New York’s Tibetan community protest outside the United Nations three weeks after Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation, calling for renewed international attention to Tibet.
Lobga Rangzen chose perhaps the world’s most recognizable symbol of international diplomacy as the place of his death. Dressed in traditional Tibetan clothing, he planted a Tibetan flag on the sidewalk across from the entrance to the the United Nations headquarters in New York on July 2. There, he set himself on fire, livestreaming his self-immolation on Facebook. His final act was intended to draw attention to Tibet’s decades-long struggle under Chinese rule.
Rangzen, 52, was born in Tibet and fled to India in the 1990s, where he lived as a monk before immigrating to the United States in 2006. Over the next two decades, he became an active member of New York’s Tibetan community. His self-immolation was the first known by a Tibetan on U.S. soil.
The protest came one day after China implemented its Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress. Amnesty International argued that the legislation further institutionalizes assimilation policies targeting Tibetans, Uyghurs, Mongolians, and other ethnic minorities while expanding the legal basis for transnational repression.
Although Rangzen’s self-immolation was intended to draw international attention to Tibet, the response from the very institution he chose to stand before was limited.
Rangzen’s choice of site was carefully considered. For more than seven decades, Tibetans have looked to the United Nations in hopes that the international body would address China’s rule over Tibet. The Tibetan government first appealed to the U.N. in 1950 after Chinese forces entered Tibet. Although the issue reached the General Assembly, the organization took no immediate action. After the People’s Republic of China assumed China’s U.N. seat in 1971, Tibet gradually disappeared from the organization’s political agenda.
For Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute and lecturer in political science at Columbia University, Rangzen’s decision was a direct appeal to the international community rather than to Beijing. “Instead of choosing the Chinese consulate, he purposely chose the United Nations as his site of protest,” Dorjee said. “The U.N. is the institution that is supposed to represent the international community’s promotion of peace, defense of human rights, and protection of cultural rights. I think he went to the U.N. because it was an appeal to the international community.”
At a U.N. press briefing the day after the self-immolation, spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric described the incident as “absolutely tragic” and expressed condolences, but did not mention Tibet or the political message behind Rangzen’s protest. Beyond that brief acknowledgment, neither the United Nations nor most governments issued substantive public responses to an act intended to draw renewed attention to Tibet.
For many Tibetans, that silence reinforced a long-held frustration. “The fact that the U.N. spokesperson refused to mention Tibet reaffirms the suspicion of the Tibetan community that the U.N. has been silent on the Tibet issue,” said Dorjee.
Amnesty International was among the few international human rights organizations to publicly respond. “Our thoughts are with everyone who knew and loved the man who has died and the broader Tibetan community,” said Sarah Brooks, Amnesty International’s deputy regional director for Asia. 
“Self-immolation as a protest by Tibetans has persisted for many years, and it does not happen in a vacuum,” she added. “It reflects the depth of desperation felt by people who see no other way to draw attention to ongoing human rights violations.”
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani also acknowledged Rangzen’s protest, saying he was “heartbroken” by the death. “No one should feel that such a desperate act is the only way to make the world listen,” Mamdani wrote on X. “New York stands for the dignity and human rights of all people.”
Why Tibet Has Faded From the International Agenda
Although Rangzen’s self-immolation drew international headlines in the days immediately following his self-immolation on July 2, attention quickly faded. Yet demonstrations continued. In New York, Tibetans gathered regularly outside the United Nations and the Chinese Consulate, while solidarity protests and prayer vigils were organized by Tibetan communities in India, Europe, and cities across the United States. 
For many activists, the brief burst of media attention underscored a larger challenge: how to keep Tibet on the international agenda once the headlines move on.
Three Tibetan youth activists affiliated with Students for a Free Tibet chained themselves to the vehicular entrances of U.N. headquarters, demanding that the organization publicly address Rangzen’s protest and ongoing human rights concerns in Tibet. The activists blocked U.N. vehicles before being arrested on charges of disorderly conduct and refusal to disperse. Hundreds of members of New York’s Tibetan community gathered outside the U.N. in support.
Among those arrested was Tsela Zoksang, campaigns director at Students for a Free Tibet. 
“His final act took place outside of the United Nations, a building that generations of Tibetans have stood outside of for 67 years in exile, calling on it to uphold its mandate of protecting peace, freedom, and human rights,” Zoksang said. “In the case of Tibet, it has failed miserably.”
For Dorjee, the issue is not simply whether the United Nations responds, but what those responses represent.
“The statements that have come from the U.N. are inadequate, for sure, but they are not ineffective,” he said.
The General Assembly adopted resolutions on Tibet and U.N. human rights experts raised concerns in 2023 over the separation of an estimated one million Tibetan children into state-run boarding schools. Those interventions have produced few immediate policy changes, yet Dorjee argued that even limited statements from international institutions remain significant.
“It may not lead to direct changes on the ground immediately, but what it does is it denies legitimacy to the Chinese government,” he said. “It denies legitimacy to Chinese rule over Tibet.”
For many Tibetan advocates and scholars, the United Nations’ muted response to Rangzen’s protest reflects a broader shift in which Tibet has steadily receded from the organization’s political agenda while China’s influence within international institutions has grown. Those concerns extend beyond Tibetan advocacy groups. A March 2026 report by the U.S. House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party argued that Beijing has expanded its influence across the U.N. system through growing financial contributions, leadership positions in U.N. agencies, participation in peacekeeping operations, and networks of state-linked organizations active in U.N. forums. The report argued that these efforts have enabled China to shape discussions on issues it considers politically sensitive, including human rights. 
China has rejected allegations that it improperly influences the United Nations, while many scholars note that the organization’s decisions ultimately reflect negotiations among its member states rather than the actions of any single country. Nevertheless, the House committee’s findings added to a broader debate over how major powers shape international institutions.
Dorjee said China’s growing diplomatic and economic influence has made many governments increasingly reluctant to criticize Beijing’s policies in Tibet – and elsewhere.
He pointed to Beijing’s diplomatic efforts in Africa, Latin America, and the Pacific Islands, where 10 countries have shifted diplomatic recognition away from Taiwan over the past decade. Dorjee argued that similar economic and political leverage has discouraged governments from speaking more forcefully on Tibet.
“China uses the influence or the attraction of trade to get countries to turn their back on Taiwan,” he said. “This is precisely the same tactic they try to use on Tibet as well.”
However, Dorjee believes China’s influence is only part of the explanation for Tibet’s diminishing international visibility.
“People are basically giving their lives in order to make their voices heard,” he said. “Tibetans have felt for a very long time that their suffering is being ignored by the world. The repression inside Tibet has intensified while international attention has declined.”
articles.summary: Loga Rangzen’s self-immolation was intended to force Tibet back onto the international agenda. Instead, it exposed the challenges Tibetans face amid China's growing global influence.

articles.title: Indian Army’s Integrated Battle Groups Are Crystallizing ‘Cold Start’ Doctrine
articles.full_text:
Given the uncertainty in the region’s escalation ladder, IBGs may be the answer if the need for a quick ground retort were to arise.
Indian Army soldiers near the Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh, India.
“Let me be clear that we cannot fight the next war like we fought our last,” said late General Bipin Rawat, then the Indian Army chief, in 2018. Rawat, who later became India’s first Chief of Defense Staff (CDS), spoke of four transformation efforts that he initiated in the Indian Army, one of which was the creation of Integrated Battle Groups (IBGs) for swift strikes. This was finally realized on July 1, when the Indian Army formally raised the first five IBGs and a Fire Support Group with long-range firepower. The new units are under the Eastern Command’s 17 Mountain Strike Corps facing China and located in two states, Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim. This enables the Indian Army to launch a blitzkrieg option. The China focus underscores where India sees its biggest threats.
The process is expected to take a year to complete. Eventually, IBGs will also be created in other sectors.
IBGs are meant to be agile, all-encompassing strike formations that can mobilize at a short notice of 12-48 hours. An IBG has around 5,000 personnel, which places it between a typical brigade (3,000-3,500) and division (10,000-12,000). Headed by a major general-rank officer, the key factor is that an IBG has all elements incorporated— infantry, armor, artillery, air defense, logistics, and so on—making it self-sufficient for swift action. Each IBG would be tailored on three Ts — Threat, Terrain and Task — as stated by officials in the past.
The doctrine and concept of IBGs have been extensively test-bedded and validated under the Yol-based 9 Corps on the Western front and the 17 Mountain Strike Corps during exercises. However, the larger modalities and the formal sanction from the government were quite delayed, so much so that in January 2025, then-Indian Army Chief Gen. Upendra Dwivedi said that a timeline was difficult to give because “wherever the bureaucracy gets involved, it will take time.” He added: “We are hopeful that by 2025, we will either create this IBG or cancel this project completely.” With the formal government sanction letter now issued, the process has commenced.
The initial ideation on IBGs was heavily focused on Pakistan, especially given its continued support for cross-border terrorism and the prevailing “no war, no peace” scenario.
However, the initial IBGs raised are facing China and that too on the eastern front, and not the Ladakh sector where the two countries have seen significant tensions since the 2020 standoff that is still underway. It is in sync with India’s recent focus on strengthening military posture and defenses in this axis given China’s increased activity and provocations in the eastern sector, and its advantage in asymmetry in areas facing the 3 Corps area. The topography and terrain in the region being mountainous makes swift mobilization a challenge for India, and an IBG gives the maneuverability for quick shallow ingress to hold swathes of territory in case of any misadventure by the People’s Liberation Army.
The one resounding lesson from the 2020 standoff with China is that Beijing only talks when it is at a disadvantage and the other side holds leverage. China started serious negotiations toward ending the standoff only after the tactical actions by the Indian Army along the North and South Banks of Pangong Tso in late August 2020. The 3,488-km-long Line of Actual Control (LAC) between India and China is divided into three sectors — the western sector spanning Ladakh, the middle sector comprising Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, and the eastern sector, comprising Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh.
The IBGs are organized on similar lines to the Combined Arms Brigades (CAB) of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), created as part of its 2017 reforms. Like the IBG, the CAB consists of 5,000-6,000 personnel and brings together various strike and support elements. Since the 2020 standoff, the PLA has deployed CABs in Tibet facing Eastern Ladakh.
The IBGs also find mention in the Indian Army’s Land Warfare Doctrine 2018, which states that when forced to prosecute a conventional war, all combat operations will function as IBGs, under the command of a combined arms operational headquarters.
The IBGs fit into the overall transformation of the Indian Army in tune with the realities of changing warfare. This effectively formalizes and also upgrades the long espoused “Cold Start” doctrine. Its existence was acknowledged by Rawat in January 2017. Cold Start was formulated from the debacle of Operation Parakram, launched after the terrorist attack on the Indian Parliament in 2001. The Army’s strike formations that were deep in the hinterland took weeks to mobilize, resulting in a cascade effect — loss of the element of surprise, the international community stepping in, and Pakistan resorting to nuclear signaling. Cold Start was seen as an instrument to make space for swift conventional operations under the nuclear overhang of the subcontinent.
The IBGs follow several other transformative initiatives rolled out by the Army in the last year, post-Operation Sindoor in May 2025. They include Rudra Brigades, Bhairav Battalions, Shaktibaan drone regiments and Divyastra drone batteries for the Regiment of Artillery. Last September, current Army Chief Gen. Dhiraj Seth, then a lieutenant general and heading the Southern Army Command, observed that with the Rudra brigade, the “time has come to change the cold start to cold strike one.” The IBGs certainly give a new impetus to this.
As witnessed during Operation Sindoor, the days of large-scale mobilization are over, with conflict moving to long-range, precision strikes from standoff ranges. Large-scale boots on the ground and ground maneuvers across borders seem passé from recent conflicts. However, given the uncertainty in the escalation ladder in the subcontinent, IBGs may be the answer if the need for a quick ground retort were to arise.
While Rawat’s initiative as army chief finally takes shape, his bigger effort, the reorganization of the military into Integrated Theater Commands as India’s first CDS, is now moving forward.

articles.title: Keep an Eye on China’s AI Governance Offensive
articles.full_text:
Beijing’s intensifying efforts to shape international norms on AI are aimed at catching up on the technology and exporting China’s illiberal values.
China’s President Xi Jinping (front center, in blue suit) poses for a group photo with other world leaders at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, China, July 17, 2026.
Beijing’s intensifying efforts to shape international norms on AI are calibrated to promote itself as a responsible global leader, but they are largely self-serving, aimed at catching up on the technology and exporting China’s illiberal values. Democracies need to get their act together in response.
President Xi Jinping delivered a keynote speech at the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance on July 17, making the case for the promotion of AI globally “for the positive, for good and for humanity.” He called for “a people-centered approach,” saying that “AI is an important driver for shared prosperity and common security” that required states to join hands “to build a just and equitable system for global AI governance.”
So Xi said all the right words. After all, China has never been short on its rhetoric. At last year’s edition of the conference, Premier Li Qiang made a strong case for global regulations governing AI using language designed to appeal to the Global South.
Noting the vast opportunities and challenges that come from the adoption of new technologies, Xi raised four points on AI development and governance: he promoted openness, collaborating, and sharing; recognized the various risks associated with AI adoption and the resultant need for AI always to be under human control; encouraged inclusiveness and the promotion of mutual learning between civilizations; and called for true multilateralism and an important role for the United Nations as well as a consensus-based governance framework in writing new global rules and technical standards.
His emphasis on international cooperation and openness has definite appeal. But it also appears to be somewhat self-serving, as China still depends on others. Henry Gao, a professor of law at Singapore Management University, said that China “wants access to global models, talent, chips, research, open-source ecosystems and technical knowledge because that is what it needs at this stage.” Alexander Evans, former cyber head at Britain’s Foreign and Commonwealth Office and former adviser to then-Prime Minister Boris Johnson, similarly noted that China needed international cooperation because “no country has complete vertical control.”
Xi’s opposition to “overstretching the national security concept in the field of AI” is a rather brazen effort to target U.S. restrictions on allowing China to access the United States’ AI technology. This is particularly rich considering Beijing’s own role in securitizing crucial assets such as trade, data, finance, markets, and access to rare earths – areas where China has deliberately created advantages for itself.
Much of the speech was aimed at the Global South. These nations will appreciate Xi’s call for international cooperation to help them with capacity building to avoid AI capability gaps and bridge existing digital divides. But they should not be fooled: Xi’s efforts are geared toward exporting what it considers responsible norms, rules, and standards, which will pay no heed to universal principles such as human or political rights.
Xi has convinced some regional blocs to support China’s vision by saying that, in the next five years, it will assist developing countries “with 5,000 opportunities in AI training and seminar programs “and “develop international AI application cooperation centers with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the League of Arab States, the African Union, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and BRICS.” It’s too early to say how this will play out and whether these organizations will endorse the emerging Chinese version of the AI order.
China is already globally exporting its tech, such as 5G network gear, drones, smart cars, and renewable energy equipment. Democracies cannot afford for it to succeed similarly with AI.
In his speech, Xi also announced the establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization for facilitating international cooperation on AI governance and development. On July 16, 29 countries – including, Pakistan, Russia, Malaysia, and Indonesia – became founding signatories. This is an impressive achievement for China, but its future remains to be seen.
Remember that China’s efforts in global governance of other domains haven’t always borne fruit. China and Russia proposed a draft Treaty on the Prevention of the Placement of Weapons in Outer Space and of the Threat or Use of Force Against Outer Space Objects in 2008 and a revised text was introduced in 2014, but there haven’t been many takers. Even those countries that have argued for legally binding mechanisms did not support the treaty. This may show how China’s AI governance journey could pan out.
While countries should be concerned that without any regulations, AI will do more harm than good, it is also necessary to come up with the right norms and rules. Allowing China – an illiberal, authoritarian, and aggressive great power with a penchant for centralization and hegemony – to determine the rules for AI governance is likely to be dangerous everywhere, including in the Global South. Xi’s speech should sound the tocsin to liberal powers across the world to get their act together. These powers need to collectively strengthen AI governance, including by promoting ethical and responsible use of the technology, before China can write the global AI rulebook.
This article was originally published in ASPI’s The Strategist.

articles.title: How South Korea’s Africa Pledges Are Faring on the Ground
articles.full_text:
In western Uganda, a project funded by the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) serves as a test case for what South Korea can offer the continent.
Participants in the program “Support for Vocational Training Schools for Persons with Disabilities and Raising Disability Awareness in Western Uganda,” funded by KOICA and KFHI.
In early June, foreign ministers and senior representatives from 50 African countries gathered in Seoul for the first Korea-Africa Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, the follow-up mechanism promised at the inaugural Korea-Africa Summit of 2024. At that summit, Seoul pledged to expand its official development assistance (ODA) to the continent to $10 billion by 2030, alongside $14 billion in export financing. The June meeting closed with a joint statement reaffirming those commitments and a proposal to convene a second summit in 2029. 
Notably, the initiative has survived the most turbulent political transition in South Korea’s recent history. Conceived under the previous conservative government, the Africa pivot has been carried forward by the progressive administration that followed, which framed the June gathering as part of its pursuit of diplomatic diversification. Two years in, the architecture to back up the Korea-Africa summit is visibly taking shape, and it belongs to no single administration.
Skepticism, however, has shadowed the initiative from the outset, and it is not unfounded. Africa still accounts for a mere 1 to 2 percent of South Korea’s trade and investment, a shortfall acknowledged openly at the 2024 summit itself. The agenda at the foreign ministers’ meeting this June, which ranged from critical minerals to supply chain resilience, looked like an inventory of what South Korea seeks from the continent rather than what it offers. Observers have pointed out that South Korea is a latecomer replicating the summit diplomacy of China and Japan, and that pledges made at such gatherings have a well-documented tendency to outrun actual disbursement. Judged by communiqués alone, it remains an open question whether South Korea’s engagement with Africa amounts to anything more than resource diplomacy in the language of development.
Nevertheless, summit halls are a poor vantage point from which to assess a development partnership. A more instructive view can be found some 10,000 kilometers from Seoul, in the districts of western Uganda, where a project funded by the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) has spent the past two years testing what a distinctly South Korean contribution might look like. The field is not minerals or megaprojects but one of the least contested and most neglected corners of the development agenda: vocational training for persons with disabilities. 
The project, implemented with a Ugandan partner organization and the National Council for Persons with Disabilities, supports students with disabilities at three vocational institutes across districts as they train in trades ranging from tailoring and carpentry to welding and hairdressing. The support itself is deliberately unglamorous: tuition, training materials, assistive devices, and preparation for Uganda’s government-certified trade examinations, which allow workers to earn a living in their chosen craft.
The project’s second-year results exceeded most of its target indicators. In the first year, 146 students with disabilities enrolled across three technical institutes; 145 remained in training. The goal is that graduates will convert certification into employment or self-employment – and that surrounding communities will come to regard such an outcome for persons with disabilities as ordinary rather than exceptional.
The project may look small compared to South Korea’s pledged $10 billion in funding. Disability-inclusive development generates no minerals, secures no shipping lanes, and produces few headlines; it is absent from the playbooks of the great power competition now unfolding across the continent. Why does such a modest project in an overlooked area merit attention in a discussion of grand strategy? 
In a conversation with the author, Kim Hyo-je, deputy country director of KOICA’s Uganda office, acknowledged the underlying reality: persons with disabilities are “the most marginalized among the marginalized,” a population overlooked not only by geopolitics but, all too often, by mainstream development programming itself. That double neglect, however, is an opening. If South Korea’s declared comparative advantage in Africa is its own development experience, then technical and vocational education, which served as an engine of the country’s postwar transformation, is arguably where that experience translates most credibly when extended to the population most systematically excluded from it. It signals, in a way that no critical minerals dialogue can, that the partnership is not organized solely around extraction.
The setting matters as well. On paper, Uganda’s disability legislation is among the more progressive on the continent, but the gap between statute and implementation is wide and, in places, widening. The 2020 revision of the Persons with Disabilities Act quietly dropped the earlier requirement that no less than 10 percent of educational expenditure be committed to special needs education. Tax incentives for employers of persons with disabilities have been diluted from a 15 percent reduction under the 2006 Act to what amounts, under current tax law, to a 2 percent deduction. The statutory instrument required to operationalize the employment quota has never been issued. In such an environment, where implementation of existing policy is the need of the hour, patient, field-level cooperation can make a meaningful difference.
Suppose, however, that the donor exits tomorrow. This is the question that every development project must eventually answer, and the honest response is that no one can be certain what would remain. Any project claiming otherwise should be treated with suspicion. What can be said is that this initiative has structured itself around that eventuality rather than ignoring the possibility. Instead of building parallel structures, it works through Uganda’s own statutory disability council. Instead of simply delivering assets, it has cultivated a coalition of local disability organizations intended to carry coordination and advocacy beyond the funding cycle. A small ICT hub nearing completion in Kasese illustrates the logic: the project financed the basic renovation, a local disability union furnished the space, and the national council secured the equipment. No single actor owns it, and therefore no single actor’s departure can close it.
Needless to say, none of this guarantees sustainability, and the uncertainties do not all originate in Uganda. South Korea’s own ODA architecture is in flux: civil society partnership schemes are being restructured, and multi-year projects can see their planned scope narrowed midstream. A pivot measured in decades will have to reconcile the long horizons that inclusion requires with the short cycles in which aid is budgeted and rebranded. It is in that tension, not in the size of the next pledge, that the seriousness of Seoul’s Africa policy will be tested.
When leaders reconvene for the proposed 2029 summit, the temptation will be to announce larger numbers. The better measure of the partnership will be whether the commitments of 2024 actually materialized on the ground. In western Uganda, the 145 students with disabilities who stayed in training, along with the certificates, workshops, and livelihoods that will follow, offer one early answer.

articles.title: Beyond a ‘Non-Red’ Supply Chain, Taiwan Should Export a Drone Ecosystem
articles.full_text:
To build a real “drone shield,” Taiwan cannot merely export hardware or components.
A drone on display at the Taipei International Aerospace  Defense Industry Exhibition at the Nangang Exhibition Center in Taipei, Taiwan, Sep. 20, 2025.
Taiwan’s government has made drone development and exports a national priority, with a particular emphasis on Taiwan’s role in the “non-red” supply chain: drones and components free of Chinese units. Taiwan’s Executive Yuan has framed this goal as part of Taiwan’s effort to become an Asia-Pacific hub for “democratic drone supply chains.” The policy reflects lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war, Taiwan’s own need to strengthen deterrence against China, and growing demand among countries and firms globally worried about the security risks of Chinese-made systems.
The logic behind this move is obvious: Chinese firms, especially DJI, still dominate the global commercial drone market, even as the U.S.  Department of Defense has stated that DJI systems pose potential national security threats. Such security concerns have created opportunities for alternative suppliers. Taiwan’s “non-red” drones are often more expensive than Chinese competitors, but the market is beginning to emerge. Taiwan’s drone exports have surged in Poland and Czechia, with possible links to wartime usage in Ukraine. Recent trade data also showed a record sale of Taiwanese drones to Saudi Arabia. 
Taiwan has advantages in the global drone market. Its semiconductor, ICT, battery, and precision manufacturing sectors give it a strong foundation for drone production. Its small and medium enterprises can move and adapt quickly. Industry leaders and politicians increasingly speak of the sector as a possible “drone shield,” a next-generation complement to Taiwan’s “silicon shield.”
However, if drones are to become a real shield that connects Taiwan more deeply with the world, Taiwan cannot merely export hardware or components; it needs to export an entire drone ecosystem.
First, in the military domain, the drone itself is only one part of overall combat effectiveness. A serious drone capability also requires operator training, simulation systems, testing fields, certification standards, logistic pipelines, secure communications protocols, software update channels, and compatibility with partners’ weapon systems. These aspects determine whether drones can be used flexibly under real battlefield pressure. 
Taiwan’s military has already begun moving in this direction. The army has formed drone battalions in several combat zones, and its drone training center has been upgraded into an Unmanned Systems Training Command responsible for education, testing, evaluation, and standards. But the key point here is whether Taiwan can build and export a complete doctrine, training, testing, and sustainment system that is insulated from Chinese interference. 
Second, drone design and algorithms are deeply shaped by operating environments. Taiwan’s geography offers unusually rich testing conditions. The Taiwan Strait brings strong winds and humidity. Taiwan’s cities combine intertwined residential and commercial spaces with communication dead zones. The island also has high-salt sea air, afternoon thunderstorms, and steep mountains. Taiwan could use its own geography as a living laboratory for drone testing, training, and adaptation. 
Third, Taiwan must make “non-red” more than a slogan. Some reporting has worried that not all Taiwan-made drones are free of Chinese components. If Taiwan wants to compete on trust rather than price, it needs credible tracing, testing, documentation standards, and certification mechanisms that foreign buyers can understand and examine. 
Fourth, Taiwan should more actively develop and export the legal and regulatory side of drone use. Taiwan is not at war yet, and both the military and civilians are already using drones more frequently. As a democracy, Taiwan has an opportunity to show how drone governance can balance civil empowerment, public safety, and national defense. 
In Taiwan, the Civil Aviation Administration has rules covering drone registration, operator certification, activity applications, insurance, and flight restrictions. These regulations should be examined and updated regularly with the advance of drone technology and practice. Meanwhile, they can also become part of Taiwan’s exportable knowledge: how a democracy integrates civilian drone use, emergency response, commercial innovation, and security concerns without treating every drone operator as a suspect.
The early signs of such an ecosystem are already there. Civil defense groups such as Kuma Academy have started drone-related training. Disaster-response organizations and local fire departments are using drones for rescue and emergency operations. Drone soccer is also spreading into schools and youth programs. These efforts are still small, but they show that drones are becoming part of Taiwan’s society and the foundation of the ecosystem.
These aspects are where Taiwan can build a long-term advantage in the drone ecosystem. It will be difficult to beat Chinese competitors purely on cost, but Taiwan can compete on trust, adaptability, training, certification, and democratic governance.
Three steps would make this strategy more concrete. First, Taiwan could consider building overseas maintenance, training, and testing hubs. Second, Taiwan could develop a transparent non-red certification system. Third, Taiwan should integrate civil defense, disaster response, education, and commercial users into its drone policy rather than treating them as separate from national security. These efforts would strengthen Taiwan’s economic security, defense cooperation, and international relevance, making the “drone shield” become more than a slogan.

articles.title: Amnesty: Deadly Pakistan Air Strikes on Kabul Drug Rehab Center a Possible War Crime
articles.full_text:
The human rights organization’s new report found “no evidence of Pakistan’s claims” that the site hit on March 16 was a military target.
Four months after calling on Pakistan’s authorities to explain how and why they targeted a Kabul drug rehabilitation center on March 16, killing at least 269 civilians, Amnesty International has published a new investigation calling for the attack to be investigated as a possible war crime. 
The organization found no evidence to support the Pakistan military’s claims that Omid Rehabilitation and Treatment Center was being used to store weapons and ammunition or for other military purposes at the time of the attack. The air strikes violated the special protection afforded to healthcare facilities under international humanitarian law, as well as the principles of distinction, precaution and proportionality designed to protect civilians.
“The attack on the Omid Center constitutes a serious violation of international humanitarian law – possibly amounting to a war crime. Given the widely available information that the site had been used as a medical facility for more than a decade, this reflects a major failure in military planning by Pakistan that led to a significant loss of civilian life,” said Isabelle Lassee, Amnesty International’s acting regional director for South Asia.
“This was a lethal failure by Pakistan to comply with its obligation to do everything feasible to verify whether the target was a military objective. Pakistan must urgently conduct a transparent, thorough, independent, and impartial investigation into the attack – especially the decision-making process that led to the targeting of the facility – and make the results public.
“Where sufficient evidence exists, competent authorities should prosecute any person suspected of criminal responsibility, including under the doctrine of command responsibility.”
The attack was one of a series of air strikes conducted by the Pakistan military inside Afghanistan since the escalation of cross-border hostilities with the Taliban in October 2025. Between January and March 2026 alone, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) documented more than 750 civilian casualties, with 372 killed and 392 others injured in Afghanistan. The June 28 airstrikes in Paktya, Paktika, and Kunar provinces killed at least 28 civilians according to UNAMA. 
While there is no consolidated figure for civilian casualties in Pakistan, media reports indicate that at least seven civilians have been killed through mortar shelling originating from Afghanistan territories.
“All parties to the conflict must respect international humanitarian law and take all feasible precautions to protect civilians and civilian objects, with particular care afforded to medical facilities and other specially protected sites. Failure to investigate serious violations, such as the attack on the Omid Center, shows an alarming disregard for international law and risks entrenching impunity, leading to further unlawful operations and loss of civilian life,” said Lassee.
Amnesty International analyzed and verified more than 60 photos and videos, most of which were captured in the immediate aftermath of the attack on the Omid Center, including videos released by Pakistan’s military to support its claim that the site was being used as a storage facility for weapons and ammunition. The organization also reviewed more than 30 satellite images of the area, as well as verified videos documenting the operations at the Omid Center prior to the attack.
Amnesty International conducted 11 interviews, including with employees and former employees of the Omid Center and the adjacent Ibn-e-Sina Hospital. Interviewees also included individuals who visited the center immediately after the attack and victims’ family members. Some of the interviewees witnessed the strikes, and some were also involved in the evacuation effort.
On July 9, Amnesty International contacted the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Pakistan to request details about what the government has done to investigate any failure in targeting, and whether those involved in the process were held to account, including any information to substantiate their claim that the target was a “weapon and ammunition store.” No response had been received at the time of publication.
Prohibition of Attacks on Medical Facilities
The principle of distinction in international humanitarian law requires parties to distinguish between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives. Deliberate attacks against healthcare facilities and on their personnel are specifically prohibited, unless a facility is being used outside its humanitarian function. When there is doubt as to whether medical facilities are being used to commit acts “harmful to the enemy” – the only case in which they could lose their protected status – they should be presumed not to be so used.
In a post on X the day after the strike, Attaulah Tarar, Pakistan’s federal minister for information and broadcasting, claimed that the Pakistan military had targeted: “technical support infrastructure and ammunition storage facilities” in two locations in Kabul (one of them being the Omid Center). He also claimed that secondary detonations indicated that large ammunition depots were hit in the strikes.
Videos and photographs of bomb remnants shared directly with Amnesty International were analyzed by the organization’s weapons experts, who concluded that at least one of the munitions used was a Takbir precision-guided bomb. This finding is consistent with statements by the Pakistani military that precision-guided munitions were used in the strike, suggesting that the attack was the result of a deliberate targeting decision.
The Omid Center was established in 2016 on the site of a former NATO base. It originally operated as a vocational training facility for people being treated for substance dependence. After the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the site was expanded into a 2,000-bed treatment center for people with drug-dependence problems. Ibn-e-Sina Hospital, which provided essential healthcare services to Omid Center patients, is also located on the site.
There is a wide range of publicly available information on the Omid Center’s work, including a 2023 Al Jazeera documentary showing patients undergoing treatment at the center.
Amnesty International identified at least two large in-local-language signboards, located above the main gate and inside the camp, clearly indicating that the location was a rehabilitation and treatment center. The organization also verified a video recorded in 2025 and captured inside the center, showing some of the hangars where patients were housed, and analyzed satellite images of the Omid Center between April 2023 and March 15, 2026. On March 13, just three days prior to the attack, imagery shows large groups of people present.
“The Pakistani authorities should have known the facility was a civilian object and that any aerial attack could result in large-scale civilian casualties. Even if the Pakistani military had any reliable information of military use, it was clear that the civilian harm would be excessive,” said Lassee.
The strikes occurred at around 9 p.m., just as the evening tarawih prayers for Ramadan were being concluded, according to people who spoke to the organization. On the night of the attack, according to several interviewees who worked in the center, more than a thousand patients were housed there.
Under international humanitarian law, attacking forces have an obligation to do everything feasible to verify whether their intended target is a military objective and, if there is doubt in this respect, to refrain from launching an attack or to cancel or suspend it. Even if a medical facility is being used for non-humanitarian purposes, an attack can only be justified after an effective warning has been issued and ignored. Amnesty International found no indication that any warning was issued, and the timing of the attack at evening prayers ensured civilian presence and left no opportunity for evacuation.
In his post on X, Tarar, Pakistan’s information minister, included several videos that he said corroborated the Pakistani military’s claims that the site was being used to store weapons and ammunition.
Amnesty International’s open-source investigators and weapons experts analyzed these videos, as well as evidence directly received from local sources and online. The videos consist of black and white drone and fighter aircraft feeds that show the air strikes from various angles. None of these videos, nor footage gathered from ground sources, allow the identification of conclusive evidence of weapons, ammunition, or other explosive goods stored in the area. The footage does not show secondary explosions immediately following the strikes, which would constitute evidence of a possible ammunition storage.
“Our investigation strongly indicates that this was not a legitimate military target under international humanitarian law. The ‘evidence’ Pakistan has made public so far does not rebut the conclusion that this was an unlawful attack causing harm to civilians and civilian objects,” said Lassee.
Digital evidence and witness testimonies indicate that at least three locations within the site were heavily damaged or destroyed as a result of the air strikes.
Satellite imagery from March 13 shows the Omid Center three days before the strikes. The east and west sides of the complex are separated by a controlled gate. Many people are visible on the east side of the gate in the imagery, which according to testimony is the main living area for patients.
The March 23 satellite imagery shows three heavily damaged and burned areas. The video posted by Tarar shows three of the impacted buildings being struck: the large building in the northeast and two buildings in the northwest. Satellite imagery also shows heavy burning and destruction in the southwest.
At one of these locations, the destruction included a large hangar situated in the northeast of the site. Several interviewees said that the site housed patients undergoing treatment, as well as the kitchen and dining hall. Videos and photos captured in the immediate aftermath of the attack and during the evacuation process indicate that the dead bodies were mostly recovered from this area.
A second location, in the northwest of the site, was used by Taliban security personnel and for food storage, according to several interviewees. The third location, in the southwest of the site, was, according to several sources, used for storing items such as coal, wood, and essentials such as clothing. It also accommodated a tailoring center.
articles.summary: The human rights organization’s new report found “no evidence of Pakistan’s claims” that the site hit on March 16 was a military target.

articles.title: The Limits – and Dangers – of the China-Russia Partnership
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Mathieu Boulègue – senior fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA) and co-author of “The China-Russia Meta Threat: The Architecture of Authoritarian Power” (CEPA 2026) – is the 518th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
How have China-Russia relations changed since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022?
I think the relationship evolved significantly after 2014 and Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine, rather than in 2022 per se, after the full-scale invasion. The weight of international sanctions and Moscow’s growing isolation pushed Russia closer to China. This consequently forced the Kremlin to replace Western dependence with dependence on Beijing and effectively created a new form of over-reliance. 
Over-reliance applies to economic subsidies, investments, and in the military sphere, to the procurement – legal and illegal – of dual-use and military technology, spare parts, and equipment. Supply chain dependency is particularly evident in microelectronics, semiconductors, circuitry, and machine-building tools used to sustain Russia’s war machine. Now the issue for Moscow is that trading one dependence for another is not ideal, but they don’t have much choice but to court China for continued support. 
Examine the “asymmetric interdependence” of China-Russia economic relations. 
The report we recently published underscores the idea that Russia can only be a “junior partner” to China, and never an equal. No amount of great power propaganda from either side can hide the fact that Russia needs China more than China needs Russia. 
Such a relationship, far from being “no limit,” is also quite fragile. The Russian leadership is perfectly aware of the increasingly asymmetric nature of bilateral relations. Meanwhile, Beijing must navigate the intricacies of using Russia as a barking dog while avoiding antagonizing Moscow or bruising Putin’s ego. Call it genuine authoritarian diplomacy. 
Military cooperation might be the area where Russia is the least dwarfed by China, mainly because Beijing is in a listen-and-learn mode. 
Analyze the “parallel play” nature of military cooperation between China and Russia.
“Parallel play” is an interesting concept, reflecting how kids in early childhood tend to play side by side but never fully together. I think it illustrates precisely how Russia and China approach military cooperation at large – interaction without the full extent of actual interaction. 
Western analyses generally tend to assume Russia-China military relations should take the form of what we see at NATO level for instance, and we tend to placate known concepts of cooperation such as “interoperability” or “strategic alliances.” Beijing and Moscow don’t need any of that to have meaningful military cooperation. 
Western-style interoperability is not something they are trying to replicate. They drill together, conduct joint patrols and overflights, etc. But it does not mean they are seeking to go further with joint security guarantees, integrated command and control, or joint operations. Actually, there are areas where their respective military interests may clash, such as in Africa, Central Asia, or the Arctic.
Identify the obstacles to closer China-Russia security ties. 
It’s important to frame Russia-China relations by what they don’t do together rather than by how they cooperate. Friction points, limitations, and obstacles in this relationship equally define the nature of their interaction. There are several obstacles in defense and security ties that can be made out. 
First, historical mistrust. There’s a long history of mistrust, especially from the Russian side, regarding military-technical reverse engineering and technology theft. Furthermore, Moscow is none too happy about perceived Chinese inroads in what the Kremlin defines as its “sphere of influence,” for instance in Central Asia and in the Arctic.
Second, the absence of shared strategic culture that could cement greater integration. Simply put, Russia thrives on military coercion, while Beijing is more subtle in its sharp power. Both countries have focused on ironing out the easy things (for instance, border issues, nonaggression, and institutional and legal frameworks) but they have not pushed for deeper military integration. From a geographical perspective, the centers of gravity are also misaligned – Russia focuses on the “NATO border,” while China focuses on the Asia-Pacific region. 
Finally, a key factor is that both Moscow and Beijing are too independent to enter an alliance that could infringe on their sovereignty and impose self-restraint. They will not be fighting each other’s wars anytime soon.
Assess the semblance of China-Russia “strategic alignment” on the trajectory of global governance and implications for the United States and European Union. 
I don’t think the alignment is “strategic” in the sense that we generally understand it. Russia-China relations are not those of NATO, the EU, or ASEAN, for that matter. It remains a fundamentally opportunistic relationship based on self-interest and scoring short-term wins. 
On top of that, they both want us to talk about it – symbols and signaling are just as crucial as substance in their relations. Beijing and Moscow want to inflate the reality of their cooperation as a form of informational-psychological warfare. This is part and parcel of how they frame their relation as anti-U.S. Yet if we look at “strategic” aspects, such as future governance models, trade, etc., it appears both countries are not aligning on long-term goals. 
It remains that even a modicum of cooperation between both countries represents a potential threat to U.S. and European interests. Exploring the limitations of the relationship should not overshadow the force-multiplier effect it has in disrupting Western governance.

articles.title: America Can’t Win the AI Race Behind Closed Doors
articles.full_text:
With China’s latest launch of frontier model Kimi K3, the U.S. must also focus on open source AI.
China just fired another shot in the most important technological competition of the 21st century – and Washington should pay attention.
Last week, Chinese startup Moonshot AI unveiled Kimi K3, a powerful open-source AI model that independent evaluators say rivals or even exceeds some of the latest systems from OpenAI and Anthropic. At nearly the same moment, Chinese President Xi Jinping stood before an international audience in Shanghai and proclaimed that artificial intelligence should not be “a solo performance by a single country but a symphony of global collaboration.”
This was no coincidence. China is making a strategic bet that open-source AI – not closed-source – will determine who wins the global technology race.
The United States should be making the same bet.
The geopolitical stakes could hardly be higher. Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming the defining technology of our era, with implications for economic growth, military power, scientific discovery, and national security. To keep its edge, Washington has focused on restricting China’s access to advanced semiconductors. Yet while the United States fights to maintain its lead in computing power, China is competing on something equally important: adoption.
History shows that the technologies that become global standards are often the ones that are easiest to use, modify, and build upon. Linux became the backbone of the internet. Android dominates the world’s smartphones. Both were open-source software; they created ecosystems rather than customers.
Chinese companies such as Moonshot, DeepSeek, Zhipu, and Alibaba are increasingly releasing powerful open AI models that anyone with the right technical skills can download, modify, and deploy. Every developer, startup, university, and foreign government that builds on those systems becomes part of China’s expanding technological ecosystem.
Meanwhile, the United States’ leading AI firms are moving in the opposite direction.
Ironically, the company called OpenAI is no longer open. Its original charter emphasized broad access and ensuring that artificial intelligence benefits all of humanity. Today its most advanced models are proprietary, accessible only through paid interfaces and cloud services. 
Anthropic has adopted a similar strategy, arguing that keeping frontier AI closed is necessary for safety. But commercial considerations appear to be the more compelling explanation.
Safety considerations for such powerful tools deserve rigorous attention. But concentrating the world’s most important technology inside a handful of private corporations creates risks of its own. Artificial intelligence has become increasingly controversial because so much power is being concentrated in so few hands. 
Fortunately, this is not the only path forward.
Open-source models are rapidly becoming more efficient. They increasingly require less computing power and cost less to operate. That means lower barriers for startups, universities, hospitals, and manufacturers, and broader participation across the economy.
Open-source models foster competition and innovation while closed-source ones hinder it. Startups can customize open-source models for specialized industries. Researchers can inspect them for flaws. Hospitals can run them securely without transmitting sensitive patient data to outside companies. Defense agencies can audit their behavior rather than relying on the black boxes of closed AI. Security researchers can identify vulnerabilities before adversaries do.
Perhaps most importantly, open-source AI democratizes innovation itself. Some of the internet’s greatest breakthroughs did not come from established technology giants. They came from unexpected innovators building on open foundations. Nobody predicted that Linux would become the operating system powering much of the global internet. Nobody foresaw Android’s dominance when it began as an open-source project. The same generative innovation is possible with artificial intelligence – but only if the underlying technology remains accessible.
This is not simply an economic argument. It is a democratic one. When only a handful of companies control the models, the computing infrastructure, and increasingly the information people consume, transparency becomes more difficult, competition weakens, and public trust erodes. Open systems allow independent experts to examine how models work, identify bias, improve security, and hold developers accountable in ways proprietary systems simply cannot.
The United States still possesses enormous advantages. It leads the world in advanced chips, venture capital, research universities, entrepreneurial talent, and high-performance computing. But those strengths will matter only if they translate into broad national capability rather than remaining locked behind proprietary walls.
If Washington allows short-term corporate incentives to dictate long-term national strategy, it risks repeating a familiar mistake. Closed-source models may maximize revenue for a few companies, but they do little to spread innovation throughout the broader economy. Worse, they create an opening for Chinese open-source models to become the world’s default platform.
China has recognized that global influence comes not merely from building the best AI, but from building the AI that the world chooses to use.

articles.title: Security Issues Are Overshadowing Kashmir’s Worsening Climate Crisis
articles.full_text:
Kashmir’s mountains are going to keep getting hotter whether anyone notices or not.
Popular perceptions of Kashmir center on soldiers, checkpoints, and decades-old fights over land. Sometimes tourism edges into the discourse. Far less attention is paid to the fact that Kashmir’s mountains are heating up rapidly.
A new study published in Nature’s Scientific Reports pulled together and analyzed 45 years of weather records from 1980 to 2024 and collected surface temperature records from ten India Meteorological Department stations. It found that the high mountain towns of Pahalgam and Gulmarg, which are also famous tourist sites, have warmed by nearly a full degree Celsius in just the last 20 years. One town, Bhaderwah, is heating up even faster at roughly 0.3 degrees per decade. And the nights are warming fastest of all. 
Meanwhile, down in the flat lowland city of Jammu, temperatures have barely moved. Some seasons there have even gotten a little cooler.
Scientists have a name for this pattern: elevation-dependent warming. Simply put, the higher up a mountain you go, the faster it warms. This happens for a simple reason. Snow is white and bounces sunlight back into space. When snow melts away, it uncovers dark rock and dirt underneath, and dark surfaces soak up heat instead of bouncing it away. Less snow means more heat, which means even less snow. It is the same thing scientists have already found happening on the Tibetan Plateau, the giant high plain north of the Himalayas. Kashmir is  as much a part of that story – but it rarely gets talked about.
This is partly because of logistics. It is hard to maintain, much less to expand weather stations in Kashmir, thanks to its checkpoints, restricted roads, and internet shutdowns. But it’s also a dynamic of Kashmir’s contested status – and not for the obvious reasons. Money and attention follow whatever the world already agrees to worry about. In international discourse, Kashmir is often treated primarily as a tale of “conflict” or “repression,” rather than a “climate” or “environment” issue. 
As a result, Kashmir is under-represented in global discussions of the warming Himalayan region, even though some researchers, journalists, and local advocates have long highlighted the region’s environmental and climate impacts. And because Kashmir’s climate gets less attention, it also doesn’t get the funding, the research teams, or the adaptation help that “hotspot” regions get.
A person in Kashmir uses a tiny fraction of the energy an average person in the United States or Europe uses. They didn’t build the factories or drive the cars that heated up the planet. But they are the ones watching the snow disappear earlier every year. A farmer plants his crops based on when the water usually arrives, and now it arrives late, or all at once in a dangerous flood, or barely at all. 
But this isn’t only Kashmir’s problem. The mountains of the wider Himalayan region hold the third-largest amount of frozen freshwater anywhere outside the North and South Poles. Up to 2 billion people depend on rivers originating in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, and these rivers are sustained by annual ice melt. When the ice and snow don’t come back in the winter, that means reduced water flows into the rivers powering and feeding much of South Asia.
There are three steps to take, right now, to begin addressing Kashmir’s climate crisis. 
First, scientists need real support to study Kashmir’s mountains the same way they already study Nepal and the rest of the Himalayas, or the rest of India. Whatever they learn should be shared openly (like the Scientific Reports paper) in open access, followed by funds allocation for mitigation and adaptation.
Second, stop treating demilitarization and climate adaptation as separate conversations in the Kashmir region. They are the same conversation, because who gets to gather information and who gets to act on it are both, in the end, questions of power.
Third, when countries meet at big climate conferences and talk about who should pay to help places already hurt by climate change, Kashmir needs to be part of that conversation – both from the climate justice side as well as colonialism side. Someone has to ask directly: who pays to fix the water systems and rebuild after floods in a place still caught in conflict?
Kashmir’s unresolved future cannot be an excuse for ignoring what is happening to its mountains right now. Kashmir’s mountains are going to keep getting hotter whether anyone notices or not. The glaciers are not waiting for a diplomatic settlement, and neither should the people whose water and lands depend on them.

articles.title: Transnational Repression, Organized Crime, and Conflict in Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
A conversation with Phil Robertson, a Bangkok-based human rights advocate.
Phil Robertson, the director of the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates.
Chinese dissident Zhang Xinyan was detained by authorities in Thailand last week while boarding her scheduled flight from Bangkok to Canada for resettlement, despite holding a refugee visa from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and all required approvals from Ottawa.
Human rights groups immediately leapt to her defense, adding there are three more Chinese dissidents – Bai Zhaodong, Tan Yixiang, and Zhou Junyi – currently being held in Thai detention centers who were at risk of being forcibly returned if local authorities bow to pressure from Beijing.
Phil Robertson, director of Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates, returns to Beyond the Mekong to speak with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about their plight and the region-wide issue of transnational repression.
“If they, these four refugees, are sent back, including Zhang and others, they would face persecution, arrest, likely torture and detention, and long prison terms,” he said.
Robertson said Zhang Xinyan’s detention had again raised concerns in the United States, European Union, Australia, and Canada, which was expected to lead diplomatic efforts in securing her release. Their plight was also reminiscent of the 40 Uyghurs that Thailand forcibly repatriated to China last year.
“If Thailand, at the last minute pulls back a case like this, because the autocratic dictatorship [in China] has demanded the return of their people, it raises concerns about whether Thailand has any seriousness in the protection of refugees,” he said.
Bangkok-based Robertson, who has 30 years of experience working in human rights, also speaks about organized crime, human trafficking networks, and scam compounds in mainland Southeast Asia, as well as cross-border relations between Thailand and Cambodia.
He said both countries are suffering, particularly economically, as the border remains shut after they fought a bitter six-month conflict across the frontier last year, ending in a December truce.
But Robertson says Cambodia has not done enough to end the scourge of organized crime – a key plank in the ceasefire – and has failed to hold accountable the country’s business tycoons, some of which have been named and sanctioned by the United States and others for their ties to scam compounds.
“They continue to be too big to touch,” he said, adding the crackdown is selective and Cambodia was trying to create an impression for the international community that it was tackling organized crime while trying to maintain the bigger, well connected scam centers.
“The international community right now is not buying it,” he said.

articles.title: Does Myanmar Still Have One Government to Recognize?
articles.full_text:
Much of the world still views Myanmar through a narrow diplomatic lens that cannot encompass the full political complexity of its conflict.
Last month, Myanmar’s new military-backed government rejected a request from the Philippines’ Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro to meet with the country’s detained civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, citing her prison sentence. Days later, Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2021 coup and anointed himself president in April, traveled to Laos on an official bilateral visit, his first to an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member state since the coup.
Although ASEAN itself has not officially recognized the new government, nor accepted the result of the election held in December and January, it still structures every visit and appointment around the notion that the junta is Myanmar’s sole government.
That is usually interpreted as ASEAN being cautious, compromised, or slow to react to the situation on the ground inside Myanmar. It instead reflects a diplomatic practice that recognizes one government per territory. Instead of asking whether ASEAN should recognize the military regime, or which of Myanmar’s competing authorities it might recognize instead, a more useful question may be whether looking for one government to recognize is the best or only way to think about the situation.
ASEAN’s founding non-interference norm took for granted a settled order of single territorial states protected from outside interference. This was codified as a principle in the 1976 Treaty of Amity and Cooperation, but the founders did not foresee a situation in which a member has a contested government.
International law distinguishes a state’s existence from recognition of its government. States continue to exist under contested or divided control without losing statehood. Myanmar is not the only case. Somalia has sustained divided control for decades, and Libya has been contested by rival governments since 2014. Afghanistan’s seat at the United Nations has been frozen since 2021. The gap exists in diplomatic practice, which treats a settled state as the default because it is the more common case.
The statistics on Myanmar show how the gap has widened. As of mid-2026, the military regime administers a territory covering between a fifth and a third of the country, albeit nearly all the major population centers. This includes areas where it maintains only a military presence with no administration. Beyond this, close to half the country has slid into a form of “warlordism,” with power fracturing into rival centers rather than converging on one single entity. The Arakan Army administers nearly all of Rakhine State, and it maintains its own independent relations with Bangladesh, although the latter states that this does not amount to diplomatic recognition.
The junta, the National Unity Government (NUG), and ethnic resistance organizations, whether or not they are aligned with the NUG, are all establishing competing centers of authority, each running their own initiatives in parallel rather than competing to be recognized as the sole government. The NUG’s own claims about how many townships it controls have shifted and been difficult to verify. In March it formed a new coordinating body with four ethnic armed organizations, in an effort to consolidate administrative control.
Describing these developments as simply how Myanmar’s politics currently works prompts an obvious objection: armed control of a territory does not automatically confer a mandate to govern it That standard, applied literally, would also implicate the NUG, whose presence on the ground depends on an armed wing, the People’s Defense Force, that it had to build after the coup, just as the junta’s authority depends on the Myanmar armed forces. But the junta’s control and the NUG’s electoral mandate are different types of claims, and neither claim resolves who should be held responsible for what has already happened, nor excuses the actions taken to retain or regain control.
Refusing to deal with an armed group does not alter the reality on the ground; it only changes which entity the external actor is willing to call the government.
Prospects for a political settlement under the “one government” model remain remote, yet diplomatic interactions are still centered around this framework. Take, for example, the Myanmar seat at the United Nations. Since a decision-making process designed for a single government cannot resolve a case without one, the U.N. Credentials Committee’s inability to choose between the junta and the NUG has simply defaulted to the current occupant.
China maintains the most consistent contact with a coalition of the biggest non-signatory ethnic armed organizations. It has not actually accepted the “one government” model and it is unclear whether Beijing even needs a single government to pursue its strategic and economic interests in Myanmar. Instead, China is pursuing local deals with individual armed groups rather than any unified outcome, since groups enjoying real autonomy already have little reason to cede ground in negotiations with Naypyidaw. For instance, the Arakan Army is currently seeking confederal status along the lines of the autonomous Wa State, instead of taking part in a federal union.
ASEAN’s stance resets with each rotating chair, and the actions of its members have not converged. Theresa Lazaro to meet with the country’s detained civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, citing her prison sentence. Days later, Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2021 coup and anointed himself president in April, traveled to Laos on an official bilateral visit, his first to an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member state since the coup.
Although ASEAN itself has not officially recognized the new government, nor accepted the result of the election held in December and January, it still structures every visit and appointment around the notion that the junta is Myanmar’s sole government.
That is usually interpreted as ASEAN being cautious, compromised, or slow to react to the situation on the ground inside Myanmar. It instead reflects a diplomatic practice that recognizes one government per territory. Instead of asking whether ASEAN should recognize the military regime, or which of Myanmar’s competing authorities it might recognize instead, a more useful question may be whether looking for one government to recognize is the best or only way to think about the situation.
ASEAN’s founding non-interference norm took for granted a settled order of single territorial states protected from outside interference. This was codified as a principle in the 1976 Treaty of Amity and Cooperation, but the founders did not foresee a situation in which a member has a contested government.
International law distinguishes a state’s existence from recognition of its government. States continue to exist under contested or divided control without losing statehood. Myanmar is not the only case. Somalia has sustained divided control for decades, and Libya has been contested by rival governments since 2014. Afghanistan’s seat at the United Nations has been frozen since 2021. The gap exists in diplomatic practice, which treats a settled state as the default because it is the more common case.
The statistics on Myanmar show how the gap has widened. As of mid-2026, the military regime administers a territory covering between a fifth and a third of the country, albeit nearly all the major population centers. This includes areas where it maintains only a military presence with no administration. Beyond this, close to half the country has slid into a form of “warlordism,” with power fracturing into rival centers rather than converging on one single entity. The Arakan Army administers nearly all of Rakhine State, and it maintains its own independent relations with Bangladesh, although the latter states that this does not amount to diplomatic recognition.

The NUG’s own claims about how many townships it controls have shifted and been difficult to verify. In March it formed a new coordinating body with four ethnic armed organizations, in an effort to consolidate administrative control.
Describing these developments as simply how Myanmar’s politics currently works prompts an obvious objection: armed control of a territory does not automatically confer a mandate to govern it That standard, applied literally, would also implicate the NUG, whose presence on the ground depends on an armed wing, the People’s Defense Force, that it had to build after the coup, just as the junta’s authority depends on the Myanmar armed forces. But the junta’s control and the NUG’s electoral mandate are different types of claims, and neither claim resolves who should be held responsible for what has already happened, nor excuses the actions taken to retain or regain control.
Refusing to deal with an armed group does not alter the reality on the ground; it only changes which entity the external actor is willing to call the government.
Prospects for a political settlement under the “one government” model remain remote, yet diplomatic interactions are still centered around this framework. Take, for example, the Myanmar seat at the United Nations. Since a decision-making process designed for a single government cannot resolve a case without one, the U.N. Credentials Committee’s inability to choose between the junta and the NUG has simply defaulted to the current occupant.
China maintains the most consistent contact with a coalition of the biggest non-signatory ethnic armed organizations. It has not actually accepted the “one government” model and it is unclear whether Beijing even needs a single government to pursue its strategic and economic interests in Myanmar.
